articles.title: Help Fund Our First Issue: Limited Edition Icon Keychain Sets
articles.dek: The limited-edition ICON KEYCHAIN SET is more than our first product. It is a way to help fund Issue One—and a physical reminder of who believed in ARCHVE from the beginning.
articles.author: ARCHVE Magazine

image.alt: Monkey holding ARCHVE keychain packaging and keychains

articles.text: We want to come out strong with our first issue. Not halfway. Not rushed. Not built through underpaid creative labor or favors we can never properly return. We want Issue One of ARCHVE MAGAZINE to establish exactly what this publication can become: ambitious, beautifully designed, carefully produced, and filled with stories that deserve to be preserved. Creating something at that level requires more than an idea. There are printing and production costs. There are writers, photographers, filmmakers, designers, editors, and other independent creators whose contributions deserve to be compensated fairly. There are stories to develop, images to produce, pages to design, and physical issues to manufacture. We understand that building ARCHVE correctly will require real resources—not only for the first issue, but for every issue and creative project that follows it. So, we decided to raise funds. We could have simply asked people to donate, but that did not feel like enough. If someone was willing to give ARCHVE a piece of their support, we wanted to give them a physical piece of ARCHVE in return. That idea became the **ICON KEYCHAIN SET**. These are not inexpensive promotional items made to be forgotten in a drawer. Each keychain was created as a high-quality, three-dimensional, double-sided PVC rubber object—something durable, tactile, and immediately recognizable as part of the ARCHVE world. The designs transform our visual identity into something supporters can carry every day. What previously existed on a screen or printed page now becomes a physical object attached to someone’s keys, bag, camera case, or wherever else they choose to keep it. It is small enough to travel anywhere, but meaningful enough to represent the beginning of something much larger. The ICON KEYCHAINS are **limited edition**. Once this original release is gone, it will remain attached to this exact moment in ARCHVE’s history: the period before the first physical issue, when the magazine was still being built through belief, experimentation, long hours, and support from the people who saw its potential early. Owning one means more than purchasing merchandise. It means becoming part of ARCHVE’s foundation. Every keychain directly supports the development of Issue One and helps us move closer to the kind of publication we believe creators deserve. It helps cover production, strengthens our ability to work with more contributors, and allows us to build toward a future where the writers, photographers, videographers, designers, and artists involved can be paid fairly for what they bring to the magazine. We do not want ARCHVE to become another company that talks about supporting creatives while depending on their unpaid labor. If this publication is going to advocate for artists, it must also respect the value of their time, knowledge, and work. This first release is one step toward making that possible. Every owner of an ICON KEYCHAIN will also receive exclusive access to future ARCHVE events and media campaigns. As the magazine expands into physical releases, screenings, exhibitions, collaborative projects, and new creative experiences, the people who supported us at the beginning will continue to be part of what comes next. The keychain becomes proof of early belief—a small membership object connecting its owner to the growing ARCHVE community. We are still at the beginning. Issue One has not yet reached people’s hands, our future events are still being imagined, and many of the stories ARCHVE will eventually document have not found us yet. But beginnings matter. Years from now, when ARCHVE has grown into the publication and creative institution we believe it can become, these keychains will represent the moment before all of that happened. They will belong to the people who helped give the idea enough momentum to become real. For everyone giving us a piece of their support, this is our way of giving you a piece of us. **A limited object from the beginning of ARCHVE—and your invitation into everything that comes next.**

articles.title: What the f*ck is ARCHVE?
articles.dek: ARCHVE is aiming to document Art, Records, Culture, Humanity, Visions & Expression from people all over the world. We believe theres already so much media based around big people, and big stories going on in the world, but, there's so much more out there that just simply isn't being documented.
articles.author: Adrian Medina, Founder, ARCHVE Magazine
articles.text: ARCHVE is a magazine—but that answer feels too small. It is a public archive for the people, ideas, images, sounds, and stories that deserve to exist somewhere permanent. It is a place for discovery, creative experimentation, and genuine human expression. Most importantly, it is the print magazine I have always dreamed of creating. For as long as I can remember, I have wanted a platform where I could showcase cool people doing cool things. Music, art, fashion, film, spirituality, personal stories, strange ideas, obscure interests—anything created or experienced with enough passion to make someone else stop and pay attention. “Cool” does not have to mean famous. It does not have to mean profitable, verified, connected, or approved by an industry. Sometimes the coolest person in the world is creating alone in a bedroom, working a regular job, living in a city nobody pays attention to, and making something incredible without an audience. That person still deserves to be documented. The problem is that much of modern media is structured around status. The same major artists, celebrities, companies, and cultural moments are discussed repeatedly because attention has already validated them. Publications cover what is guaranteed to generate traffic, and algorithms continue circulating the names people already recognize. Meanwhile, an entire world of human creativity remains invisible. There are people everywhere with unbelievable stories, rare talents, unconventional perspectives, and fully developed ideas who may never receive meaningful coverage. Not because their work lacks value, but because they do not have enough followers, industry connections, social credibility, or money to make traditional media acknowledge them. ARCHVE is being created to challenge that system. I want this to be one of the few media platforms where access is not determined by popularity. It should never feel like an exclusive club or a pay-to-play publication where recognition is reserved for whoever can afford it. Anyone should be able to submit an image, video, story, piece of music, unfinished idea, or personal obsession and know that it will be considered for what it actually is—not dismissed because of who did or did not create it. Talent exists before recognition. A story matters before the person telling it becomes famous. ARCHVE should be the place that understands that. The goal is not simply to feature people. It is to give them a meaningful piece of media they can carry forward—something that introduces their work to a new audience, strengthens their presence online, and creates a permanent record proving that their ideas existed. There is already enough noise on the internet. ARCHVE is supposed to create focus. When someone enters this world, I want them to encounter ideas they would not have found through an algorithm. I want them to discover a musician from a city they have never visited, read the story of someone they would have otherwise passed on the street, or become fascinated by an interest they had never considered. The platform should feel unpredictable but intentional: a place where completely different people can exist beside one another because they share the same underlying quality—something worth documenting. I AM A DESIGNER. Not to sound cocky, but I genuinely believe in my abilities. I understand layout, typography, color theory, image-making, photo manipulation, composition, and the emotional power of visual communication. Design is not simply something I do when I am hired. I regularly spend more than 12 hours a day creating, even when there is no immediate return, because I honestly love the process that much. ARCHVE gives that obsession a purpose. I want people to send me their photographs, stories, music, films, memories, and unfinished ideas so I can sit in my room and build worlds around them. I want to take raw material from another person’s life and transform it into a composition that feels considered, beautiful, and completely specific to them. Every story should have its own visual identity. Every article should feel like an art piece. Every physical issue should be something people want to keep instead of something they skim once and throw away. A musician should not receive the same predictable layout as a filmmaker. A deeply personal story should not be flattened into the same template as a fashion editorial. The design should respond to the subject—their personality, environment, history, and creative language. If someone trusts ARCHVE with their story, it should be treated with care. That is the difference between filling pages and building an archive. Right now, ARCHVE is barely getting started. At this stage, I am the founder, writer, designer, editor, creative director, web developer, and almost everything else the magazine needs. I know that will not always be the case. My larger dream is to build ARCHVE into a company capable of employing hundreds of creative people: writers, editors, designers, photographers, filmmakers, researchers, interviewers, developers, culture scouts, and people whose future roles may not even have names yet. I want to create the kind of company I have always wanted to work for—one that respects creative labor and actually pays artists fairly. Too many businesses depend on the passion of creative people while treating that passion as an excuse to underpay them. ARCHVE cannot claim to protect creativity while exploiting the people responsible for it. The company must grow without abandoning the values that made it necessary. ARCHVE will not be defined by how famous its subjects are. It will be defined by how deeply it sees them. It will not document culture from above. It will grow from within it, alongside the people actively creating it. So, what the f*ck is ARCHVE? It is a magazine for people who have something real to share. It is a creative platform without a velvet rope. It is a physical record of ideas that might otherwise disappear. It is proof that an unknown person’s story can be treated with the same care, imagination, and importance as the biggest name in the world. It is still becoming—and that is what makes this the perfect time to begin documenting it.

articles.title: 10 of the sexiest summer films of all time
articles.author: Olive Parker
articles.text: Summer is a temporary escape from everyday life, where the usual rules are suspended. Days are long, hot and languid, but often boring. We spend more time outside, in the sun. We take our clothes off at the beach and the pool. We lounge in parks and gardens. We eat, sweat and, often, lust. Emotions are heightened; summer is the season of transgression. The relationship between sun and sin can be seen in many iconic films. Some of the greatest romances unfold over the course of a summer, while others use the heat and freedom of the season to explore the darker sides of sex and obsession. I have selected ten personal favourites that approach summer’s hedonism in more perverse ways. Some are raunchy, even X-rated, while others are more fascinated by heated glances and the eroticism of a single touch. Each film, for me, captures the beauty and intensity of a long, hot summer – albeit one that leaves its characters changed forever. LAST SUMMER (2023) Queen of controversy Catherine Breillat’s most recent film, Last Summer, follows a married lawyer who embarks on an affair with her teenage stepson. Starring Léa Drucker and Samuel Kircher, and set in an affluent Parisian suburb at the height of the season, Last Summer reworks the 2019 Danish film Queen of Hearts into a luminous tragedy of passion and transgression. Returning after a decade away from filmmaking, Breillat proves she remains one of cinema’s great chroniclers of amour fou. Complex, humane and beautiful, Last Summer is one of the auteur’s finest works. ACCIDENT (1967) Joseph Losey’s Accident turns a languid English summer into a study of sexual rivalry. The 1967 Cannes Grand Jury Prize-winning film follows two married Oxford academics, Stephen (Dirk Bogarde) and Charley (Stanley Baker), as they compete for the affections of their student, Anna (Jacqueline Sassard). The setting is idyllic – lunches in the garden, cricket and tennis, long afternoons in the countryside – but beneath the rituals of middle-class summer leisure lies a world of jealousy, desire and deception. Harold Pinter’s screenplay turns polite conversation into a battlefield, while Losey uses the lush landscape as a backdrop for one of British cinema’s most devastating portraits of amorous infatuation. CRAZED FRUIT (1956) There is longing in every frame of Kō Nakahira's Crazed Fruit, a sensational 1956 summer drama, a ‘Sun Tribe’ film often described as Japan's answer to Rebel Without a Cause. Set around the coast of Kamakura, it follows the introverted Haruji and his gregarious older brother, Natsuhisa, as they compete for the affections of the alluring (and married) Eri. The characters spend their holiday sailing, waterskiing, smoking, gambling, and kissing illicitly. Years before the French New Wave popularised its restless visual style, Nakahira was experimenting with exhilarating camerawork and editing, giving the film an extraordinary sense of youthful momentum. Crazed Fruit is a treasure, brimming over with barely-veiled summer sexuality. CLAIRE‘S KNEE (1970) Any one of Rohmer’s summer films could have found a place on this list, but I’ve opted for Claire’s Knee, the fifth of his Six Moral Tales and one of his most erotic works. Holidaying by Lake Annecy, Jérôme (Jean-Claude Brialy) becomes acquainted with Laura (Béatrice Romand), the teenage daughter of a neighbour of an old friend, who introduces him to her half-sister, Claire (Laurence de Monaghan). Though engaged to be married, Jérôme finds himself hypnotised by Claire’s youth and beauty, becoming fixated on the seemingly trivial object of her knee. Shot by regular collaborator Nestor Almendros, the French lakeside scenery glows as Rohmer’s characters spend the long summer days developing crushes and discussing the intricacies of desire. LA PISCINE (1969) Is La Piscine the most iconic summer film ever made? Jacques Deray’s Côte d’Azur psychological drama stars Alain Delon and Romy Schneider as a couple whose holiday is interrupted by the arrival of an old acquaintance (Maurice Ronet) and his sultry eighteen-year-old daughter, played by Jane Birkin. One of European cinema’s most iconic former couples, Delon and Schneider reunited – at Delon’s entreaty – for the film, bringing a palpable eroticism to their characters’ volatile relationship. Luca Guadagnino later reworked the story as the 2015 film A Bigger Splash. With its rich colours, modernist design, Michel Legrand score, bronzed stars and those Courrèges costumes, La Piscine encapsulates 60s cool. STRANGER BY THE LAKE (2013) Stranger by the Lake is an explicit, sun-soaked gay thriller written and directed by Alain Guiraudie. The Cannes prize-winning film takes place at a lakeside cruising spot in southern France, where Franck, played by Pierre Deladonchamps, falls for Christophe Paou’s seductive but dangerous Michel, even after witnessing Michel drown his lover in the lake. What follows is a dark, intoxicating romance, notable for its ample full-frontal male nudity and unsimulated sex scenes. Guiraudie’s critically acclaimed erotic drama is an enthralling depiction of lust and obsession. JAMÓN JAMÓN (1992) A sensual slice of Spain from 1992, Bigas Luna’s romantic tragicomedy launched the careers of Penélope Cruz and Javier Bardem, who wouldn’t begin dating until they reunited on the set of Vicky Cristina Barcelona – itself a worthy contender for this list – 15 years later. The young leads are magnetic and impossibly attractive. Sexy, funny and full of food, this absurd, tempestuous romance unfolds over a sweaty Spanish summer, as the daughter of a prostitute falls for an aspiring bullfighter. Luna revels in the sensual pleasures of bodies, landscapes and appetites pushed to delirious extremes. JE T‘AIME MOI NON PLUS (1976) Je t’aime moi non plus is Serge Gainsbourg’s singular 1976 drama, written, directed and scored by the French provocateur himself, with his iconic song echoing throughout. Jane Birkin stars as Johnny, an androgynous truck-stop waitress who falls for the rugged trucker Krassky (Joe Dallesandro), despite the fact that he is already in a relationship… with a man. One of the strangest and most unforgettable romances of all time follows: an outrageous yet tender tale set against the sweaty, desolate landscape of Uzège. If you don’t believe me, listen to François Truffaut, who is reported to have said, “Don’t bother going to see my film, see Gainsbourg’s. That is a work of art.” FRIVOLOUS LOLA (1998) Tinto Brass’s Frivolous Lola is a breezy softcore comedy, full of sexual frolics and flouncing around the sunny Italian countryside. The lovable protagonist Lola, played joyfully by Anna Ammirati, is determined to sleep with her fiancé, Masetto, before their wedding night, but her beau wants to wait. A series of perverted encounters occur as Lola does everything in her power to lose her virginity to literally anyone, anywhere, anyhow… Frivolous Lola is one of Brass’s most charming and fun films, unabashedly horny and full of kitschy Italian style. WILD THINGS (1998) Summer boils over in this cult-classic ‘skin flick’, one of the sexiest thrillers ever made. Set among the Floridian swamps, John McNaughton’s Wild Things follows a high-school guidance counsellor accused of rape by two female students. What follows is a labyrinthine investigation packed with increasingly outrageous revelations, featuring an ensemble cast including Matt Dillon, Kevin Bacon, Neve Campbell, Denise Richards, Bill Murray, Daphne Rubin-Vega and Theresa Russell. Pools, motels, swamps, yachts. McNaughton embraces sticky excess as the film reaches glorious levels of absurdity. Roger Ebert affectionately described it as “bad taste elevated to the level of demented sleaze”, and it is precisely this mix of unabashed camp and carnal intrigue that makes Wild Things so irresistible. Follow Olive Parker on Instagram

articles.title: Get to know Molly Santana, the emo princess of underground rap
articles.dek: Ahead of her new campaign with UGG, we caught up with the 21-year-old to chat about collabing with Drake, touring with North West and ruffling some feathers
articles.author: Isabel Bekele
articles.text: It’s hard to imagine there are many 21-year-olds having a better summer than Molly Santana. When I join our call, the rising rapper, whose past few months have included a smattering of festival appearances, viral collabs and cosigns from everyone from Don Toliver to Alysa Liu, is still recovering from her previous night’s show in London. “That’s why my voice sounds a little crazy,” she tells me, apologising through her rasp. To those tapped into the underground rap scene, Santana’s low gravel has been a familiar voice since 2021, when the Los Angeles-based artist dropped her debut EP Molly’s World, a four-track collection littered with the assertive bars and synth-heavy production she’s become known for. While that early output lured in her first generation of fans, millions more became hip this May when she joined Drake and Future on “Ran to Atlanta”, one of ICEMAN’s strongest tracks. Since its release, it has racked up over 90 million streams on Spotify and ushered Santana into the mainstream limelight. Her recent ascent makes Future’s declaration on the track feel that much more accurate: “They wanna play Molly Santana.” When listening to Santana’s glitchy rage raps, it’s easy to hear the influence of fellow experimental rappers like Playboi Carti and Lil Uzi Vert, who she cites as longtime favourites. It wasn’t all rap, though – as a kid in Southern California, Santana was a student of all genres. “Growing up, there was a lot of Paramore, My Chemical Romance and Pierce the Veil,” she says. Alongside her love for emo punk, she had an affinity for “West Coast, slower indie”, like surf-rock act Current Joys. Today, that smorgasbord of influences has resulted in a sound that’s self-assured and entirely her own. And as she makes her way out of the underground, others are taking note, too – most recently, UGG tapped Santana to star in the campaign for its Dusty Orchid Collection, which, in the spirit of embracing the unexpected, ditches the brand’s neutral colour palette in favour of a new purply-pink shade. Ahead of the campaign’s release, we caught up with Santana to chat about collabing with Drake, touring with North West and ruffling some feathers. Photography Hannah Moon How would you describe your music to somebody who’s never listened to it before? Molly Santana: I don’t ever use this word, but androgynous. I think that it’s almost polarising in a way, because when you look at me, and then you hear what I sound like, it almost doesn’t make sense, because it’s two opposites coming together and making something. To me, it feels very powerful and very feminine, but still androgynous and genderless in a way. You went to fashion school in Japan for a time. What was that experience like? Molly Santana: It was so much fun. It was such an amazing experience to be able to live in Tokyo when I was like 18, 19 years old. Those were very important memories for me to continue building the story and continue building my knowledge of the fashion world, and not just fashion, but art in general. I was the only American at my school. I think in Japan, they are focused on perfection. Their fashion is known for the architecture – the perfectionism of it is just out of this world. But it definitely taught me that I just don’t fit in the fashion industry in that role. I was taking a pattern-making and fashion design course, and it was just very intense. I love fashion, but the more I was in school, I noticed that my heart was more into music because it’s a more raw expression of yourself. There are honestly no rules when it comes to rap. Coming from the underground, it’s a very raw place. Speaking of fashion, you’re one of the faces of UGG’s new campaign for their new Dusty Orchard collection. How did that collaboration come about? Molly Santana: Ava Nirui [the creative director] had actually messaged me, and I had been wanting to work with her for a long time. I’ve been such a big fan of her and just everything that she does. I think she’s such an amazing creative force, honestly. And with UGGs, I love UGG. Everybody loves UGG. Coming from California, the Cali girls wear UGG any season, all year, that’s our thing. This is my first campaign with a fashion brand, so it was just super exciting. And I love that shade of pink. That's actually my birthday colour. So it was a perfect little match-up moment, honestly. What’s your favourite style from the new collection, and how have you been styling it? Molly Santana: I was wearing the micro in the shoe [in the campaign], but I also love the minis. Those are my favourites because I think you can wear them with basketball shorts, short shorts, baggy pants. There are just so many different ways you can wear them, so I think they’re very cost-friendly. But I also love the Mary Janes, they’re so cute. How do you feel you’ve been able to challenge people’s expectations in your career so far, especially as a young woman coming out of the underground rap scene? Molly Santana: I think all female artists feel me on this one, but honestly, even just starting out is challenging, especially in rap. It’s a very male-dominated space, so just being a female coming up in this space and following your heart, doing what you desire and being true to yourself is already challenging people’s expectations. When it comes to rap, it’s about your lyrics, it’s about your bars, and if you don’t come correct, they come at you crazy. And even if you do come correct, they’re always gonna have something to say when you’re a woman, because we’re spectacles. We’re supposed to have the attention. Whether it’s good or bad attention, you just gotta ride the wave. Who or what are some of your biggest influences fashion-wise? Molly Santana: Lady Gaga, number one. That is my north star right there. Obviously, Nicki Minaj. I think her fashion over the years has been so inspirational. I don’t think anybody has really tapped into that Japanese, cute gyaru-type style, and she made it so fun and bigger than life. I really respect her for that. Also, Michael Jackson. His fashion is just amazing. And then the fourth person I’ll say is Erykah Badu. I think her fashion is just out of this world as well. Who is your dream collab? Molly Santana: Lady Gaga and Nicki Minaj. Oh, and Rihanna. Oh my gosh, Rihanna, so bad. Speaking of collabs, your recent collab with Drake, “Ran to Atlanta”, has been blowing up. What has it felt like to see fans love it this much? Molly Santana: It just feels like a whirlwind of crazy new energy, and I’m trying to sort through it all right now. But I think that it’s been a great moment for me and my fans to share. Me and my fans really feel like a family. They’ve been riding with me for a minute, and I think it was such a crazy moment for us because now we have something to point to and be like, ‘This is why we love this girl. This is why we go so hard. This is why we continue to show up for this woman.’ There are people out there who are genuinely inspired by what I do, and that’s always been the goal. It gives me energy to have moments like that where it feels full circle, and I’m not just yelling out into the ether, into a black hole. It just felt very rewarding. You also recently announced a tour with North West. How did you two become friends, and what are you most excited about for the upcoming tour? Molly Santana: The first time I met North was actually at my first Summer Smash performance a year ago. And now this year, she performed the slot right before me, which is another full-circle moment that was just so beautiful to see. She has been showing me so much love, genuine love and support since the day that I met her, and I think it’s very rare in this rap space that girls get together and support each other. I’m just excited for this tour. I think that she is so talented and so much stronger than a lot of people who are honestly double her age. If anybody deserves to go on tour and show people what they’re about, she’s definitely one of them. She really deserves a platform because she really does work hard for it, and she rehearses every day. She’s really locked in. It’s an amazing thing to watch and see her grow. What can you tell us about your upcoming album, Black Punk? Molly Santana: I’m very excited to paint the picture and explain my standpoint on where I’m trying to lead this generation to, where I’m trying to lead the underground rap scene. I really want to be one of those people who help lead more female rappers, more children and people in this underground scene to continue taking their craft seriously and continue taking themselves seriously. And it’s gonna be powerful. This album is definitely for all the people who see themselves in me and who see parts of themselves in me, who can relate. And even for people who don’t understand anything that I got going on, this album is supposed to be very universal. I think it’s gonna ruffle a few people’s feathers.

articles.title: Are AI dating apps ushering in the era of swipeless dating?
articles.dek: As the founder of Hinge launches a new AI matchmaking app, doing away with swiping and supposedly based on "relationship science", we explore whether technology can really help us find the one
articles.author: Ruby Conway
articles.text: It’s hard to imagine the experience of dating without swiping. But ‘Overtone’, a new app from Hinge founder Justin McLeod, will soon make this a reality. Instead of split-second and often shallow decisions, the new model is based on a curated matchmaking service. The matchmaker is AI, of course, promising a tech-bro hack for compatibility – a concept that romantics, astrologists and relationship scientists have puzzled over for decades. “Arranged marriage has the same concept, but your parents are AI,” wrote one user on X. Compatibility, a longstanding buzzword relationship science, is the key criterion on which Overtone will curate its matches. “We make only the introductions that are worth making, grounded in relationship science and thoughtful reflection,“ writes McLeod. Scientists have dedicated entire careers to studying love, chemistry and attraction, and the idea that technology could know greater truths about compatibility is nothing new: the first algorithm-led matchmaking models came into use back in the 1960s. One of the earliest was TACT, or Technical Automated Compatibility Testing, which once matched a man with his younger sister – similarity isn’t always all that. But when it comes to predicting compatibility prior to meeting (after that, it's a different story), objective truths have been difficult to come by. “You can predict who's popular, but you can't predict who's compatible” – Paul Eastwick “We have some machine learning studies going back about a decade now where we've been trying to do exactly that,” Paul Eastwick, author of Bonded by Evolution and Professor of Psychology at the University of California, Davis, where he heads up research at the attraction and relationships research laboratory, tells Dazed. “You take information that people report about themselves before potential partners meet each other, and you look at their preferences and their personality and all their attributes, and you can predict who's selective, and you can predict who's popular, but you can't predict who's compatible.” While it’s not yet clear how exactly Overtone’s AI matchmaking model would work – a company spokesperson tells Dazed it is based on “the study of how people connect and what makes long-term relationships work” – Eastwick is sceptical. “If by relationship science, you mean we're going to give people a bunch of questionnaires and assess their preferences and their personalities and match people up, it doesn't work that way,” he says. “We tried that. We've tried that a billion times. You really can't predict much better than chance who's going to like whom when people sit and self-disclose.” But despite its dystopian undertones, Overtone is likely to hold some appeal to those exhausted by the worst – i.e. most time-consuming, laborious, futile and superficial – features of the modern-day dating experience: the swiping, the dead-end chats, the choice overload. Although she hates the current crop of dating apps, Indigo, 28, says she would be interested. That both parties would have to give over more information, as it seems, would hopefully make for a more considered match. Then there’s the appeal of “not having to think about it that much,” she adds, and of the app’s shift away from infinite choice, which has started to feel like its own prison. Instead, Overtone offers tech-enabled hyper-curation, an experience so frictionless that we don’t have to do anything. We can rest our thumbs, sit back and wait for a ‘perfect’ match to be presented by technology. “Will we have to wait to be told by AI that we're compatible before we fully believe it, losing trust in our own instincts, judgement and emotions?” I myself am not averse to having these decisions taken away from me. When I’ve used dating apps, I’ve been caught at my most shallow, making split-second judgements and searching for similarity rather than difference. Even if we believe we know what we’re looking for, is this level of self-actualisation actually available to us, or even possible? We might have a list of things we think we want in a partner, but research shows that when presented with a real-life person, those things often go out the window. In one study, 74 per cent of people chose to go on a date with someone who showcased two of their personal dealbreakers. Many of us have experienced being attracted to or even falling in love with people who, if we encountered them on a dating app, we wouldn’t give a second glance. But because Overtone is a dating app, after all, it’s offering an even more privatised future of dating. Down the line, will we feel, even more than we do today, that love is something we’re not capable of finding ourselves? Will we have to wait to be told by AI that we're compatible before we fully believe it, losing trust in our own instincts, judgement and emotions? Perhaps compatibility is not static or pre-determined. For Eastwick, certainly, it is something that evolves. And in many ways, it’s a beautiful thing that we can’t predict it or have it handed to us, that we have to feel our way through the world to get there. “[Compatibility] is what enables a lot of people to find relationships who are not immediately, you know, the most desirable people in the room,” says Paul. However it is you get there, you probably do have to be in the room for that compatibility to emerge.

articles.title: Inside Lin Zhipeng's sultry, summery YSL exhibition
articles.dek: The latest show by the artist Lin Zhipeng (AKA No.223) evokes the romantic atmosphere of Qixi, the Chinese equivalent of Valentine’s Day
articles.author: Emily Dinsdale
articles.text: Lin Zhipeng (AKA Finger 223), Rive Droit (2026 A feeling of summer heat radiates from Lin Zhipeng (AKA No.223)’s photographs. It’s not just the golden light permeating his work that suggests warmth; it’s the febrile sensuality. “Originally from the South, I am captivated by warm light and sultry air,” the Beijing-based photographer explains. “I often travel to southern areas and tropical destinations, so a summery aura and mood always shine through my images.” Like summer, his work contains an abundance of flowers and fruit – sweet and alluring, yet on the cusp of rotting in the heat. “[These] are recurring symbols in my photography,” the Beijing-based photographer explains. “For me, they represent transience. They are beautiful, tender, ripe and fleeting. They contain desire, growth and inevitable decay.” The artist worked with YSL’s creative director Anthony Vaccarello to curate his latest exhibition at Saint Laurent Rive Droit Beijing. Taken from his extensive archive, the pictures were selected to echo the theme of Qixi, known as Chinese Valentine’s Day, which falls every year on 19 August. This body of work reverberates with the feverish sexuality and vibrating desire that makes his work so distinct. © NO.223 (LIN ZHIPENG) & THREE SHADOWS +3 GALLERY / 编号223（林志鹏）及三影堂+3画廊 While the sliced figs, splayed grapefruit segments and lily heads with their sticky stamens are almost obscene, there’s a poetic, gentle quality to No. 223’s pictures – they are always suggestive rather than graphic. “I would describe the atmosphere of these photographs as tranquil and unrushed, imbued with understated sensuality,” he tells me. They are “laced with playfulness”. Like the spirit of Qixi, they are romantic and tender. “This exhibition interprets romance and intimate human connection through the lens of Chinese Qixi culture,” he says. “It presents gentle, subtle, and authentic love moments expressed through flowers, fruit, human bodies, and quiet interactions.” We see the heads of two figures embraced, lit by a patch of sunlight; we see a palm gently holding the flowers of Ochna integerrima with their red petals and swollen black fruits; we see the very tender flesh of someone's neck, arched in pleasure or pain. To me, there is a perfection about his pictures. But he resists this idea. “There is no such thing as a perfect photograph,” he insists. Instead, he’s drawn to “a sense of incompleteness in images – minor flaws within what otherwise appears harmonious, carrying an irreproducible emptiness. It is similar to shooting film; many imperfections emerge from outdated analogue technology, yet these blemishes hold their own charm. To embrace imperfection is a stance. I resist the overly polished completeness that prevails in our current digital era.” But, in this age of eerily flawless AI-generated images, perhaps the idiosyncrasies of analogue are the new standard of perfection. And, if not perfection, then some other sublime quality. The exhibition will be running at Saint Laurent Rive Droit Beijing until 11 September 2026.

articles.author: Adrian Medina

articles.text: Houston-based creative **Joshey D. Sowells, known as Joshey.s**, moves fluidly between styling, casting, creative direction, and talent management. His work is less defined by a single discipline than by an ability to shape the visual language surrounding a project—from the people involved to the way the final image is presented. For the **adidas x Andu.C x The Better Generation “GrassRoots” Predator Sala** collaboration, Joshey photographed the release through his own perspective before sending a selection of images our way. Those photographs became the foundation for this ARCHVE editorial. Rather than approaching the project as straightforward product imagery, we wanted to push the photographs into something more graphic, textural, and expressive—building an editorial world around the Predator Sala while retaining the energy of Joshey’s original images. The resulting series sits somewhere between campaign imagery, street photography, and independent print design: a reinterpretation of a collaboration already rooted in community. “GrassRoots” Created by **The Better Generation and Andu.C in collaboration with adidas**, “GrassRoots” centers on the relationships and experiences formed around football. The concept looks beyond the game itself, focusing instead on the environments people come from, the goals that keep them moving, and the friends and communities who become part of that journey. Mud, movement, competition and memory become recurring ideas throughout the project—the grassroots moments that exist long before anyone reaches a larger stage. The release was built around the **adidas Predator Sala**, accompanied by a wider collection of objects and printed material designed to extend the story beyond the shoe itself. The Tier 2 package included the Predator Sala, a tote bag, presentation box, red and yellow card keychain, six randomly selected stories, and a *World Newspaper*. Only **1,248 numbered pairs** were produced, a figure referencing the number of players competing across the FIFA World Cup tournament. For us, though, the strongest part of the project exists within the images themselves. A collaboration interpreted by Joshey.s, then reconstructed once more through ARCHVE. PHOTOGRAPHY Joshey.s EDITORIAL DESIGN ARCHVE / Adrian Medina

articles.title: HTX ORIGINALS: finding beauty in the violence, repetition and ritual of sport
articles.dek: An editorial by Adrian XLVII and Joshey Sowells turns athletics inside out — pairing football, boxing and tennis with corsetry, tailoring, heels and high-fashion styling to explore the beauty hidden inside the process.
articles.author: Adrian Medina
articles.text: TEXT Adrian Medina CREATIVE DIRECTION & STYLING Joshey Sowells EDITORIAL DESIGN Adrian XLVII There is nothing particularly clean about becoming good at something. Athletics are built on repetition. Sweat. Bruises. Failure. Trying something again until the body stops having to think about it. Long before the stadium lights, sponsorships and final scores, there is the process — the ugly, obsessive stretch of work that almost nobody sees. **HTX ORIGINALS** lives somewhere inside that space. Created by **Adrian XLVII and Joshey Sowells**, the Houston-based editorial takes the visual language of adidas and pulls it away from the conventional sports campaign. Instead, football, tennis and boxing become raw material for something stranger: part athletic portrait, part fashion story, part visual study of what happens when strength and beauty are allowed to exist in the same frame. Across the series, familiar sporting objects are pushed into unfamiliar territory. A football sits beside formal tailoring and sequins. Goalkeeper gloves frame a face like an accessory. A tennis racket becomes almost ornamental. Boxing gloves are paired with an exposed torso and dramatically oversized shorts, while another look places athletic branding against a corseted silhouette. Elsewhere, a flowing red skirt and heels collide with the posture and props of the football pitch. Nothing is separated neatly into *sport* or *fashion*. That tension is the point. THE ATHLETE AS A CHARACTER Much of the project’s strength comes from **Joshey Sowells’ approach to casting, styling and creative direction**. Joshey has an instinct for seeing beyond clothing alone. Casting becomes part of the styling. A face, body, pose and attitude are treated with the same importance as the garment itself. The models don’t feel interchangeable because they aren’t being used simply to display product. Each occupies a different athletic archetype. Football feels youthful and almost nostalgic. Tennis becomes poised and sculptural. Boxing becomes confrontational. The personalities shift, but they remain connected by a shared visual world. That ability to build characters is what makes Joshey particularly effective as a creative director. Instead of dressing everyone according to a single obvious interpretation of sportswear, he allows contradiction into the frame. Masculinity can be delicate. Femininity can feel physically imposing. Sportswear can sit beside tailoring. A corset can belong on a tennis court. Heels can exist next to football socks. The later images push these contrasts even further, moving between a tennis portrait constructed around black adidas sportswear and a white corset, stripped-back boxing imagery, close beauty photography and an almost theatrical football look against a glowing orange field. It makes athletics feel less like a category of clothing and more like a vocabulary. DESIGNING THE WORLD AROUND IT If Joshey built the characters, **Adrian XLVII’s editorial design gives those characters a world to live inside.** Adrian’s strength is his ability to take photography and make it feel larger than the original image without overwhelming it. The design throughout **HTX ORIGINALS** borrows from the authority of vintage sports advertising — oversized serif typography, aggressive adidas marks, tiny utilitarian credits and tightly controlled campaign information — but rearranges those references with the instincts of contemporary independent publishing. The opening **HTX ORIGINALS** compositions are particularly direct: enormous white typography cuts across deep red backgrounds while the subjects remain dominant in the frame. Instead of decorating the photography, the typography behaves almost like another physical object inside it. That balance is central to Adrian’s approach. His editorial work often relies on **scale, hierarchy and restraint**. He understands when an image needs typography and, equally importantly, when it needs almost nothing. Some pages are virtually untouched beyond a small adidas mark and restrained information running along the bottom edge. Others become fully constructed advertisements, using enormous logos, campaign titles and tightly packed credits to make newly created imagery feel as though it has been pulled from an archival magazine spread. It is graphic design being used not simply to *present* photography, but to change its context. A portrait becomes a campaign. A campaign starts resembling an old magazine clipping. An old visual language suddenly feels contemporary again. BEAUTY IS PART OF THE WORK Sports photography traditionally celebrates the result. The finish line. The winning goal. The knockout. The body at the exact moment it performs perfectly. **HTX ORIGINALS is more interested in everything surrounding that moment.** The preparation. The clothing. The personality. The strange rituals athletes build around themselves. The physical vulnerability hidden beneath performance. And maybe most importantly, the idea that beauty does not exist separately from all of that brutality. It exists because of it. A boxer’s body is shaped by repetition. A footballer's relationship with the ball comes from thousands of touches nobody watched. Grace in movement is produced through exhaustion. Style develops through identity, environment and community just as much as it does through clothes. The editorial exaggerates that relationship visually. Sport becomes glamorous without losing its physicality. Fashion becomes rougher without losing its beauty. That is why the photographs can move from an athlete standing over a football to an extreme beauty portrait seen through adidas goalkeeper gloves without feeling like two separate stories. They are both studying performance. Just from different distances. HOUSTON, REINTERPRETED There is also something distinctly Houston about **HTX ORIGINALS**. Not because it relies on obvious regional imagery, but because it carries the confidence of a city where completely different references have always been comfortable existing beside one another. Luxury and streetwear. Football and fashion. Beauty and aggression. Polish and imperfection. The title itself — **HTX ORIGINALS** — feels less like a declaration of where someone is from and more like a statement about how creative identity develops. Originality rarely appears out of nowhere. It comes from absorbing everything around you, pulling it apart, keeping what feels personal and rebuilding it into something that belongs to you. That same process exists throughout this editorial. Joshey Sowells constructs the people, silhouettes and visual performances. Adrian XLVII constructs the graphic language around them. And somewhere between the two, adidas sportswear becomes something else entirely. Not simply clothing for the athlete. But clothing for the person underneath one. **HTX ORIGINALS is an editorial about athletics, but more than that, it is about the process of becoming — and all the strange beauty that gets overlooked along the way.**
