articles.title: Houston in Polo: reframing Ralph Lauren through a city that has always dressed on its own terms
articles.dek: For a Houston-focused Polo Ralph Lauren campaign, Joshey Sowells brings together casting, styling and creative direction while Adrian xlvii builds the editorial language around the imagery — placing an American fashion institution inside a distinctly Houston perspective.
articles.author: Adrian Medina

image.alt: Houston Polo Ralph Lauren campaign editorial

articles.text: TEXT Adrian Medina MODEL CASTING, STYLING & CREATIVE DIRECTION Joshey Sowells EDITORIAL DESIGN Adrian xlvii There are certain clothes that stop belonging exclusively to the brand that made them. They get worn long enough, passed around enough, photographed enough and adopted by enough different communities that eventually they begin collecting meanings of their own. **Polo Ralph Lauren is one of them.** The pony is recognizable almost anywhere. So are the rugby shirts, striped button-downs, cable knits, caps, quarter-zips and oversized pieces that have spent decades moving between prep, sport, hip-hop, streetwear and everyday American dress. But Houston has never been particularly interested in wearing anything exactly as intended. The city takes things and bends them. Luxury gets worn casually. Sportswear gets oversized. Something traditionally polished can suddenly feel completely different once it is placed against Houston’s people, architecture, heat, cars, music and attitude. That tension became the starting point for the **Houston Polo Ralph Lauren Campaign — Editorial Work**. Rather than treating the imagery as another exercise in clean luxury advertising, the project pushes Polo through a distinctly Houston lens — shaped through **Joshey Sowells’ casting, styling and creative direction**, then extended into an editorial world through **Adrian xlvii’s graphic design**. POLO, WITHOUT THE COUNTRY CLUB Ralph Lauren has always understood the power of building a world. The clothing matters, obviously, but so does everything surrounding it: the person wearing it, the environment they occupy, the typography sitting beside them and the lifestyle an image quietly suggests. For Houston, that world changes. The fantasy becomes less about escaping somewhere else and more about recognizing elegance in the place already around you. Because Houston has its own relationship with aspiration. Here, dressing well does not necessarily mean dressing quietly. There is pride in excess. Pride in detail. Pride in looking intentional even when the silhouette feels effortless. A piece can be classic without becoming conservative, expensive without becoming delicate and familiar without becoming boring. That is where Polo makes sense. Not simply as an imported idea of American prep, but as something generations of people have already absorbed and rewritten for themselves. CASTING THE WORLD At the center of the campaign is **Joshey Sowells**, whose work across **model casting, styling and creative direction** determines much of the personality inside each frame. Casting, for Joshey, is more than finding somebody who looks good in the clothes. It is about finding the person who makes the clothing believable. The right face changes the story. The right posture changes a silhouette. The way somebody naturally occupies a garment can communicate more than the garment itself. That instinct carries into the styling. Rather than approaching Polo as something precious or overly traditional, Joshey treats the pieces as part of a larger character. Proportions, layering and attitude allow familiar Ralph Lauren codes to exist inside a more contemporary Houston context. The result avoids costume. Nobody feels like they have been dressed to imitate someone else's version of American style. They feel like themselves. And that is where the images become most interesting. CREATIVE DIRECTION AS CHARACTER Joshey’s strength as a creative director comes from understanding that a campaign cannot survive on clothing alone. There has to be a person inside it. A mood. A posture. A reason the image exists. His approach creates a visual language where the polish associated with Ralph Lauren can sit beside Houston’s more instinctive, street-level energy without one cancelling the other out. The campaign does not reject Polo’s heritage. It roughens its edges. There is a difference. A classic piece can still feel young. Something preppy can still carry attitude. A recognizable brand can enter a new environment without losing what made it recognizable in the first place. The objective is not transformation for transformation’s sake. It is context. BUILDING THE IMAGE AFTER THE PHOTOGRAPH Once the photographs exist, **Adrian xlvii’s editorial design** gives the campaign another life. Rather than treating graphic design as decoration placed over completed photography, Adrian approaches each image as the beginning of a larger composition. Typography establishes scale. Negative space creates tension. Small information systems give the imagery the authority of traditional fashion advertising. More aggressive compositions begin to resemble archival magazine pages, campaign tear sheets or forgotten printed advertisements. His broader design practice is rooted in typography, magazine layout, hierarchy and visual systems across both print and digital work. That background becomes particularly useful with Ralph Lauren because the brand already carries decades of visual history. There is no need to redesign something people immediately recognize. The challenge is deciding what to leave alone. Some photographs need little more than a mark. Others can withstand enormous typography and dense campaign information. The strongest editorial design knows when to speak and when to disappear. THE POWER OF SOMETHING FAMILIAR Fashion spends a lot of time chasing newness. New silhouette. New collection. New collaboration. New person everyone is suddenly supposed to know. But there is another kind of power in clothing that has already survived long enough to become familiar. You recognize Polo before you really study it. That familiarity gives an editorial permission to focus on something beyond the product. **Who is wearing it now?** **What does it mean here?** **What happens when the same piece enters a completely different environment?** Those questions are more interesting than simply asking whether something is fashionable. A garment does not exist in isolation. Its meaning changes depending on who puts it on. And Houston is particularly good at changing meanings. The city has spent decades taking sounds, cars, clothes, slang and aesthetics and filtering them through such a specific regional identity that they emerge as something unmistakably its own. Polo remains Polo. Houston simply wears it differently. HERITAGE DOESN’T HAVE TO FEEL OLD The strongest heritage brands carry a strange responsibility. Change too much and people stop recognizing them. Change nothing and heritage becomes nostalgia. Creative direction and editorial design offer a space between the two. You do not have to redesign the garment to make someone reconsider it. Sometimes you only have to change the person wearing it. The styling. The posture. The environment. The crop. The typography. Suddenly something you have seen a thousand times becomes worth looking at again. That is ultimately where the **Houston Polo Ralph Lauren editorial** lives. Between two visual languages. There is Ralph Lauren’s America — polished, aspirational, athletic and deeply invested in clothing as world-building. And then there is Houston’s. Louder. Hotter. Looser. More unpredictable. Still elegant, just according to its own rules. Through **Joshey Sowells’ model casting, styling and creative direction**, those worlds meet in front of the camera. Through **Adrian xlvii’s editorial design**, they continue beyond it. **Not Polo brought to Houston.** **Polo, once Houston gets its hands on it.** MODEL CASTING Joshey Sowells STYLING Joshey Sowells CREATIVE DIRECTION Joshey Sowells EDITORIAL DESIGN Adrian xlvii

articles.title: 'He never needs to drop again': The legacy of Frank Ocean's Blonde
articles.dek: 10 years ago, the Grammy award-winning artist dropped Blonde, and music changed forever. Here, fans reflect on what the album has meant and continues to mean to them
articles.author: Halima Jibril
articles.text: Frank Ocean – summer 2019 10 years ago, Christopher Edwin Breaux, known to the world as Frank Ocean, dropped his second studio album, Blonde. Released 48 hours after publishing his ambient 45-minute visual album Endless (the album he used to fulfil his contract obligations to Def Jam and Universal), the four-year-long drought, filled with cryptic Tumblr posts, letters and a library due date card with random dates, finally came to a disorienting and abundant end: two albums and a glossy accompanying magazine, Boys Don’t Cry. Endless set the internet ablaze. Launched on a live stream, where dedicated, hungry fans watched Ocean build boxes and watch paint dry over previews of instrumental music. Pitchfork's Ryan Dombal called the whole spectacle “painfully dull”. But that all got overshadowed when Blonde debuted. “R.I.P. Trayvon, that nigga look just like me”, Ocean's autotuned child-like voice sings on lead single “Nikes”. The four years between Ocean’s critically acclaimed debut album Channel Orange and Blonde saw a modern civil rights movement erupt in the US, prompted by the brutal murders of 12-year-old Trayvon Martin; Michael Brown, Eric Garner, Tamir Rice, Eric Harris, Walter Scott, Freddie Grey, Alton Sterling, and many more by the police (or in the case of Martin, a neighbourhood watch volunteer, who was aquitted of all charges and served no prison time). Blonde is not a particularly political album, but this line is both its most overly political moment and one of its most memorable – a simple, haunting recognition that Martin’s unjust end could happen to any young Black man. It’s a powerful introduction to an album that explores many themes: masculinity, drugs, family, queerness, youth, morality, self-love and self-hatred, and falling in and out of love. For many young people, it was the album they came of age to; an album so emotionally intelligent that listening to it felt like waking up for the first time. “To put it simply, Blonde gave boys my age access to a musical and emotional vocabulary that hadn't existed before,” 29-year-old Jacob tells Dazed. Blonde, in all its minimal simplicity (it mostly uses guitar and keyboard loops, albeit punctured by moments of psychedelic splendor, drawing influence from the likes of the Beach Boys and Todd Rundgren along with the R&B greats), is surprisingly difficult to describe. One thing's for sure: it is profoundly affecting. Listening to it 10 years on, it’s difficult not to think of Ocean’s brother, Ryan Breaux, who died in a car crash in 2020 at the age of 18, and who features on the album’s final song “Futura Free”. Lines like “we’ll never be those kids again” on “Ivy,” which were always true, painful reflections on the passage of time, now hurt in new and unexpected ways, all these years later. Below, fans of Ocean try their best to explain what this groundbreaking album means to them. MONTSERRAT, 28 Listening to Blonde was the first time, I was unequivocally moved by art and wanted to learn more about it. I had just turned 18 and was going on a family trip, so I downloaded the album to listen to offline. I listened to it all that spring and summer during car rides, looking out the window, and “Ivy” was my favourite song. During that time, I used to hook up with boys that pretended we were ‘just friends’ in public. The whole narrative about being loved and intimate behind closed doors really resonated with me. [The album] spoke on my terms and in my language about experiences I struggled to put into words. It was like a gateway drug to more complex artists and pieces, but it definitely changed my interests and the respect I had for music, performance and lyrics. MANNAV, 23 Blonde means everything. I got a tattoo of the helmet from the album’s shoots on my 18th birthday. I listened to it once a day religiously during COVID. I wrote essays dissecting it, held listening parties, anything to get my people [friends] involved with this album. To this day, I can name every hidden feature, every sample and interpretation; I can spatially sense when Kanye says “love” on “White Ferrari”. This album got me into paying attention to music. It got me into being proud of being really nerdy. I haven’t heard it in maybe two years purely because I committed it to memory early on. His brother’s interviews on the back end of “Futura Free” are still icebreaker questions that I ask people. “What’s one superpower you wish you had?” etc. It‘s a life-changing, seminal piece of work. I’m okay with him never dropping again. He’s done enough. This album will feel new again in several years of not listening. AMARÍ, 24 Up until that point, I only had one picture of romance, or even love, or a crush for that matter. I thought there was only one way that it could go. Then I listened to Blonde when I was 14. Frank’s entire infatuation with references to cars, religion, style and memory felt so specific to me. So niche! I remember hearing “Nikes” for the first time and getting stuck on the line about the yarmulke. I literally stopped and researched it because I was so fascinated by the idea of him talking about a boy, desire, and identity while pulling in something so deeply cultural and symbolic. He takes all of these references and filters them through this glittery, hazy, almost red-lit mind: smoking with a boy, sweat and “glitter”, memories, all of it colliding into one feeling. I think that was the first time I understood that infatuation could look and sound so beautiful. ISABEL, 27 Blonde was the first time I ever fully noticed the concept of an album. I was in secondary school when it dropped. I didn't really listen to Western music, so it was my first venture into it. My friends and I listened to it on repeat, chose our favourite songs and were mind-blown by all the featured artists as well. It’s lowkey a gateway album to other great albums. We all stanned Frank like crazy afterwards. In retrospect, we were all overreacting a bit, but as teenagers, I think it was normal. I still really like the music, but I wouldn't die over it now. It's a very sentimental album to me, though, given the amount of time I spent discussing it with friends. “Nikes” was the song we listened to together the most. And then we went to see him together at Lovebox in 2017 – it was unbelievable! He was late as fuck, and I didn't know any of the words, but he had a grip on my friends and me. I think my love for the album at the time was more about the community, but it was such a good soundtrack to our Black and gay teenage friendship. JACOB, 29 When Blonde was released, it was the last few weeks of summer before going back to my second year of university. I was 19 years old. I remember the online buzz, with Endless released and the immediate follow-up a day later: Blonde. I was a huge fan of Channel Orange, and I remember being so excited. The first time I listened to the album in its entirety was on a late-night drive with my girlfriend at the time. I remember thinking how beautiful the album was, the variety and creativity on display. If you take “Pink + White” and “White Ferrari”, I was struck by the moments of density versus how happy Frank was creating a stillness in his music. The first song that really stuck with me would have been “Nights”; the atmosphere so perfectly matched the drive, watching the sunset and streetlights passing us by. The beat switch in “Nights” might have fundamentally changed my brain chemistry; it made me consider music differently and the multitude of emotions a single song can evoke. To put it simply, Blonde gave boys my age access to a musical and emotional vocabulary that hadn't existed before. It also created a generation of softboys who endlessly speculated and crashed out on Reddit over the follow-up album that never arrived.

articles.title: North West Thinking About Working at Starbucks Next Year: 'I Want To Have a Regular Job'
articles.author: Alex Ocho
articles.text: The 13-year-old explains why she thinks she can land the gig, even as she builds out a music career. Image via Arnold Jerocki/Getty Images North West apparently wants to don that famous green apron. In a new interview with Dazed Digital for the magazine's autumn 2026 issue, the 13-year-old daughter of Kim Kardashian and Kanye West was asked by journalist Marios Mystidis what she would do if she weren't an artist, and if being a basketball player is “still on the cards.” "No, it's not. What would I be? I still wanna work. I wanna work at, like, Starbucks next year. I think I can next year 'cause I'm gonna be 14, so… I think I can. I want to have a regular job, I guess," she said. North released her debut EP, N0rth4evr, in May when she was 12. Despite her coffee shop ambitions, music is clearly not something she plans to trade in anytime soon. In the same interview, North described her ideal day: "I don't like to rest a lot. I like to get stuff done. So maybe just going to rehearsal, and then going to the studio; that's a perfect day." Elsewhere in the interview, she recalled the “worst” piece of advice she received. “To start my career later,” she said. “It's like, nah, this is my hobby, this is what I like to do, this is what I wanna do with my life." North was originally set to co-headline the Kimokawaii Tour alongside Molly Santana earlier this month. However, the 14-city tour was cancelled for unspecified reasons in late July. “I was really excited to go on tour w molly santana[.] sadly it isn’t happening anymore but i have something special for u guys. see ya soon,” she wrote in an Instagram Story at the time. Shop for North West music and merch at Complex.

articles.title: Don Toliver Brings Out Justin Timberlake for Surprise Performances of “Rock Your Body” and 'Body”
articles.dek: (Photo by Leon Bennett/Getty Images for The Recording Academy)/ (Photo by Leon Bennett/Getty Images for The Recording Academy)/
articles.author: Trey Alston
articles.text: Justin Timberlake made a surprise appearance at Don Toliver's Miami concert. Justin Timberlake is back on stage, and Don Toliver put him there. Timberlake joined Toliver as a surprise guest during the NITROUS leg of the OCTANE World Tour, a moment made all the more fitting given that Toliver's single "Body" is built around a sample of Timberlake's 2002 hit "Rock Your Body." The connection between the two songs runs deeper than a flip. Toliver has spoken openly about how much Justified, the album that originally housed "Rock Your Body," means to him. "I got a lot of fond memories of that," he said to *Billboard* earlier this year. "Justin Timberlake is always one of my favorites. Justified, that album is literally in my top 10 favorite albums of all time." The decision to sample it, he said, came from pure instinct. "I didn't think that deep into it," Toliver explained. "Hold on, this is literally one of my favorite songs of all-time. 'Rock Your Body' is one of those songs that triggers an endorphin in my body. To put those two together was so iconic for me." "Rock Your Body," produced by the Neptunes, is one of the signature singles from Justified. Timberlake also shared a video of himself watching the show from the crowd before being brought on stage. The NITROUS leg, the second phase of Toliver's OCTANE tour, kicked off August 4 in Sacramento after the first run of 31 dates sold out and pushed the tour to add 19 more cities. The leg wraps up Sept. 6 at Barclays Center in Brooklyn before the tour heads to Europe through late November.

articles.title: Isaac Nease '@_rkyves' : “The Deep End” Unfinished animation from 2025
articles.dek: An appreciation of a close friend, a limitless creative mind, and his unfinished 2025 animation, “The Deep End.”
articles.author: Adrian Medina
articles.text: Some artists inspire you through a single finished work. Others change the way you understand creativity altogether. Isaac Nease—known creatively as _rkyves—has always been the latter for me. Isaac and I have been close friends since high school, but describing him only as a friend would leave out one of the most important parts of our relationship: he is also one of the artists who made me want to create more fearlessly. Knowing him has continually reminded me that art does not have to remain confined to one format, one discipline, or one definition. An idea can become an illustration, an animation, a photograph, a piece of music, a film, or something that does not have a name yet. What matters is having the curiosity to follow it. There is something rare about watching someone close to you develop a creative language of their own. You do not only encounter the finished work—you witness the searching, the experimentation, the abandoned ideas, the unexpected breakthroughs, and all the quiet decisions that happen before anything is ready to be shown. Through Isaac, I learned to appreciate that part of the process just as much as the final result. His work has encouraged me to look beyond the limits of whatever medium I happen to be working in. It made me stop asking what kind of artist I was supposed to be and begin asking what each idea could become. That influence has followed me through everything I create. Whether I am designing, writing, building a world, directing an image, or exploring an entirely unfamiliar medium, some part of that curiosity can be traced back to the artists who made creative freedom feel possible. Isaac is one of those artists. That spirit is present in “The Deep End,” an unfinished animation from 2025. ) The word unfinished can sometimes sound like an apology, as though an incomplete work is less deserving of attention. In reality, unfinished art can reveal something a polished final piece often conceals. It allows us to see an artist in motion—testing an idea, discovering its rhythm, and building a world before every edge has been refined. The uncertainty remains visible, and that visibility gives the work its own kind of honesty. Animation makes that process especially intimate. Every moment has to be constructed. Movement must be imagined before it can be seen, and time itself becomes part of the material. Even in an unfinished state, an animation can contain intention, atmosphere, personality, and possibility. It can show us where an artist was going while preserving the traces of how they were attempting to get there. That is what makes The Deep End worth sharing. It does not need to pretend to be complete in order to communicate Isaac’s talent. Its unfinished state is part of its significance—a record of an idea being pursued and evidence of a creative mind refusing to remain still. This feature is not simply about presenting one animation. It is about recognizing the person behind it and giving appreciation while that person is still creating, experimenting, and becoming. Too often, artists receive their flowers only after the world has decided their work is important. The people closest to them already know. I have had the privilege of knowing Isaac beyond the work. I have seen the imagination, instinct, and genuine creative ability that exist behind the name _rkyves. More importantly, I have felt the effect of that creativity on my own life. His talent has pushed me to explore art in all of its forms and to trust that an artist never has to remain inside one category. The Deep End may be unfinished, but Isaac’s influence on me is already permanent. This is my appreciation for a close friend, an extraordinary artist, and someone whose work deserves to be seen—not only for what it is today, but for everything it suggests is still to come.

articles.title: Exploring Takashi Murakami's Iconic Art Style: The Superflat Revolution
articles.author: Loughercontemporary.com
articles.text: What is Takashi Murakami's Art Style? Even if you haven’t heard of Takashi Murakami, you’ve definitely seen his work. Takashi Murakami stands as a seminal figure in the contemporary art world, renowned for his vibrant and innovative artistic style known as Superflat. Originating in Japan, Superflat art represents a fusion of traditional Japanese art and aesthetics with the boldness of modern pop culture, creating a visually striking and intellectually engaging body of work. “My aesthetic sense was formed at a young age by what surrounded me: the narrow residential spaces of Japan and the mental escapes from those spaces that took the forms of manga and anime.” Takashi Murakami Interview with Esquire, August 2008 What is Superflat art? At the heart of Murakami's Superflat aesthetic lies a deliberate flattening of forms and perspectives, drawing inspiration from traditional Japanese art forms such as ukiyo-e prints. This flattening effect serves to challenge conventional notions of depth and space, creating a visually dynamic and immersive experience for the viewer. Central to Murakami's Superflat universe are his iconic characters, including Mr. DOB, Kaikai Kiki, and the whimsical flowers and mushrooms that populate his artwork. Takashi Murakami's flowers are an instantly recognisable icon worldwide. These characters, often rendered in bright colours and bold outlines, exude a playful charm that belies deeper themes of consumerism, globalisation, and otaku culture. What inspired Takashi Murakami? Indeed, otaku culture – characterised by a fervent obsession with anime, manga, and video games – serves as a foundational influence on Murakami's work. Through Superflat, Murakami explores the intersection of high and low culture, challenging traditional distinctions between fine art and popular culture. This celebration and critique of otaku culture has resonated with audiences worldwide, elevating Murakami to international acclaim. Beyond its visual appeal, Superflat art holds deeper cultural and socio-political significance. Murakami's collaborations with Western artists, fashion designers, and brands have helped to bridge cultural divides and foster dialogue between East and West. Through his work, Murakami addresses pressing issues such as consumerism, technology, and the commodification of art, sparking critical reflection on the state of contemporary society. Takashi Murakami artworks in exhibition Takashi Murakami's latest exhibition at the [Kyoto City Kyocera Museum of Art’s](https://news.artnet.com/art-world/takashi-murakami-monoke-kyoto-kyocera-2452415#:~:text=Art %26 Exhibitions-,Takashi Murakami's New Works Fill His First Japanese Exhibition in,DOB%2C an early Murakami character.) is a captivating exploration of the artist's boundless creativity and innovative vision. Featuring an impressive collection of 170 Murakami works, many of which are being unveiled for the first time, the exhibition offers visitors a unique opportunity to immerse themselves in the vibrant world of Superflat art. From whimsical characters to mesmerising floral motifs, each piece showcases Murakami's signature style and meticulous attention to detail. The global appeal of Murakami's Superflat aesthetic is evident not just in Japanese art, but in its widespread influence across various disciplines, including fine art, fashion, design, and popular culture. From his iconic collaborations with Louis Vuitton and Kanye West to his monumental sculptures and exhibitions around the world, Murakami continues to push the boundaries of artistic expression and challenge the status quo. As we delve into the captivating world of Takashi Murakami's artworks, we are invited to explore the intersection of tradition and modernity, East and West, high and low culture. Through his bold visual language and thought-provoking themes, Murakami inspires us to question, engage, and reimagine the possibilities of contemporary art in a rapidly changing world.

articles.title: Adrian47: 'How i'm going to change the magazine industry forever'
articles.author: Adrian Medina
articles.text: Magazines were once cultural objects—things people waited for, collected, displayed, traded, and returned to years later. They documented movements before history had found the language to explain them. They gave artists entire worlds to exist inside and made ordinary people feel like their stories were worth preserving. Somewhere along the way, much of that feeling disappeared. People became content. Art became promotion. Stories were shortened, simplified, and forced into familiar formats because those formats were easier to sell. Many publications began documenting only what had already been validated: the biggest name, the safest trend, the person with the most followers, or the story most likely to perform online. I want to build the opposite of that. With ARCHVE MAGAZINE, I plan to create a publication shaped by people of every kind—not only established artists, celebrities, or industry-approved voices. I want to document the person creating alone in their bedroom, the musician recording songs no label has discovered, the photographer carrying a camera through their neighborhood, the designer building an entire world without a budget, and the ordinary person with an extraordinary story they have never been given the space to tell. The future of magazines should not be controlled by who already has access. It should be built around discovery. ARCHVE will accept photographs, videos, writing, unfinished ideas, personal memories, strange interests, difficult experiences, and stories that may not fit neatly into a traditional editorial category. A submission should not need to arrive as a completed article to be valuable. Someone may send a photograph, a voice note, a sentence, or the beginning of an idea. My responsibility as an editor and creative director is to recognize what exists inside it and transform it into something unforgettable. That is one of the ways I plan to change the industry: every story will be treated as an opportunity to create art. I do not want ARCHVE’s pages to feel like information placed inside a template. I want every feature to have its own visual language. The typography, pacing, imagery, composition, and physical experience of the page should respond to the person being documented. An interview with a musician should not look identical to a story about someone’s childhood. A photo essay should not be forced into the same system as a personal confession. Each subject deserves a world built specifically around them. The magazine itself should feel less like a product and more like an artifact. I want people to keep an issue of ARCHVE because it captured something that could never exist in quite the same way again. Years from now, someone should be able to open it and understand how people were thinking, dressing, speaking, struggling, celebrating, and creating at that exact moment. Not the polished version rewritten after a movement becomes profitable—the real version, documented while it is still alive. That is why the name ARCHVE matters. To archive something is to declare that it deserves to survive. My plan is not to separate print from the digital world, but to make them strengthen one another. The website can move, evolve, and introduce people to stories instantly. Print can give those stories permanence. One can capture the present while the other protects it from disappearing. Together, they can create an experience that is immediate without becoming disposable. ARCHVE began with my own perspective, but it cannot end there. I do not want to build a magazine that only reflects my taste or my immediate surroundings. Although my story begins in Texas, the publication should have no creative border. Someone from Houston should be able to exist beside someone from another side of the world—not because their experiences are identical, but because both deserve to be documented with the same level of care. Changing the magazine industry also means changing the relationship between a publication and its audience. I do not want ARCHVE to speak down to people or tell them what they should consider important. I want the audience to help shape what the magazine becomes. The readers can also be the contributors, subjects, artists, photographers, writers, and future editors. The publication should feel like a living exchange between people rather than a distant institution deciding culture from above. I know that saying I plan to change the magazine industry forever is ambitious. It is supposed to be. Real change rarely begins with permission. It begins when someone becomes dissatisfied with what already exists and decides to create the thing they wish they could find. I cannot predict exactly how large ARCHVE will become, but I know what I want it to stand for: creative freedom, honest documentation, meaningful collaboration, and the belief that no genuine human story is too small to become art. I do not want to create another magazine people briefly scroll past and forget. I want to create something they can hold. Something they can feel. Something that introduces them to a person they would have never discovered otherwise. Something that inspires them to make their own work, tell their own story, or see their own life as worthy of documentation. The goal is not simply to participate in the magazine industry. The goal is to remind people why magazines mattered in the first place—and then build what they can become next.

articles.title: Hot couture: How will extreme heat change the fashion industry?
articles.author: Sophie Wilson
articles.text: Sweat vs style: How will extreme heat change the fashion industry? From early morning runway shows to UPF clothing and dystopian accessories, the climate crisis is having a profound effect on fashion Maiden Voyage 2026 If one accessory ruled this summer, it wasn’t raffia beach bags or bug-eyed shades. The handheld fan – frantically flapping in festival crowds, whizzing silently on public transport or draped over shoulders as a resourceful, futurist-apocalyptic form of neckwear – is now a summer staple. But what sets it apart from polka dot capri pants or split toe footwear is that it isn’t really a trend at all. It’s a crucial adaptation for living in a hotter world. Since men’s fashion week in June – when temperatures reached 41 degrees celsius in Paris – Europe’s fashion industry is no longer able to ignore the practical implications of the climate crisis. Shows (including Dior and Rick Owens) were rescheduled to the early morning to avoid blistering afternoon heat. Parasols, fans and water bottles became an essential part of the fashion editor’s toolkit. The collections themselves reflected a changing wardrobe for a rapidly changing world. At Dior’s SS27 men’s show, Jonathan Anderson showcased semi-transparent pinstriped and checked suits crafted from translucent silk chiffon. “No joking: How to dress for the inferno of summer is a real fashion issue to be dealt with everywhere,” Vogue critic Sarah Mower wrote in her Dior show report. Meanwhile, at Comme des Garçons Homme Plus the opening looks were made entirely from light and breezy striped shirting cotton. Even couture, known for heavy gowns and rich materials, was stripped back. There were transparent, airy kaftans at Fendi and sheer, sleeveless tweed suits at Chanel – light enough to fold up and pack neatly into a small suitcase. High street retailers are adapting too, with H&M recently announcing they will be designing their autumn collection out of lighter materials in anticipation of soaring September temperatures. ) At Rick Owens, design went beyond lightweight textiles to focus on utilitarian innovation. Outsized, inflatable black puffer jackets and matching trousers housed miniature electric fans to keep goths cool in the summer heat. Whether innovations like this transition from the runway into mainstream fashion remains to be seen, but it’s not enough for summer clothes to just look good anymore. Extreme heat is changing the properties we expect our clothing to have. According to Emily Gordon-Smith, content director at trend forecasting agency Stylus, innovations around cooling technologies and UPF clothing – designed to protect your skin from the sun’s powerful UV rays – will soon become a big market, but western fashion has been slow to adapt. “Consumer demand will quickly outpace brand response,” she says. “Brands like Uniqlo and Bosideng are leading in delivering real UPF innovation while cooling devices like Daiso’s neck cooler band and ByCruise’s ultra-chic and resilient handheld paper-look fan are selling out fast, but no one is owning either the traditional paper fan category nor innovating enough in the consumer tech device area.” Dior SS27 men’s Festival fashion is changing beneath the weight of the climate crisis too. Last year, London’s All Points East festival issued a dust warning, urging festivalgoers to come equipped with sunglasses, reusable water bottles and face coverings due to extremely dry and dusty conditions. Reports and photos from this month’s Maiden Voyage, Houghton and Boomtown festivals show a similarly bone-dry landscape with some attendees turning scarfs, bandanas and balaclavas into face coverings to style out these apocalyptic conditions. “It’s this added thing that people are going to think about,” says sustainable fashion advocate Brett Staniland. “You leave the house now thinking, ‘I look nice, but will I be able to breathe? Will I be too hot? Have I got a bottle of water with me? Do I have a portable fan?’” Extreme heat is impacting fashion not just sartorially, but structurally. Attendance for some shows at Paris Fashion Week men’s fell by as much as 50%, according to Staniland. Fashion is a physical industry. If people can no longer comfortably attend fashion shows, shop in person or work in uncooled studios and factories, there will be increasing disruption. Trips to the high street were down by 6.2% in the UK in June, a decline that the British Retail Consortium attributed to the heatwave. “Independent brands will suffer the brunt,” says Staniland. “This means fewer opportunities to grow their brand and give them the exposure they desperately need. Designers aren’t happy, and they’re the ones that are trying to find solutions more often than not.” Fashion will adapt, but adaptation creates its own problem. Many climate activists suggest that adaptation alone is not an adequate solution. It raises uncomfortable questions about whether fashion can respond to climate change without turning it into another consumer trend. As the fashion industry is responsible for 10% of global carbon emissions, responding by creating more products - such as cooling jackets, lighter fabrics and portable fans- risks ignoring the root cause and contributing further to the climate crisis. “The fashion industry is co-opting and using extreme heat as an opportunity to create or expand a market,” says climate activist Emma de Saram. “They're adapting to a problem that they're further perpetuating.” Additionally, heatwaves have made the wealth divide feel even starker. Not everyone will have access to state-of-the-art climate-adaptive clothing. Fashion professionals who work in hot shops and factories, rely on public transport and live in apartments without air-conditioning will suffer more. “I think it will get to a point where people start disrupting fashion weeks because it's so antithetical to everything that is required for this planet to continue in a habitable sense,” says fashion climate activist Tori Tsui. “The turning point will have to be when things get so bad that it will be akin to another pandemic, where we actually cannot operate as usual because there are literal barriers for us to do that.” Fashion has always adapted to changing environments and social norms. The difference now is that the climate is changing faster than the industry’s infrastructure can accommodate. There is a real need to pay attention to the root cause of the rising heat alongside adapting to it. There are many responses at play, but one thing is certain: fashion cannot ignore these heatwaves any longer. “The fashion industry has to contend with the fact that change is coming that's going to affect their business,” concludes Tsui, “but people are not going to stand for it. We have to be prepared for disruption.”

articles.title: The 25 Best Fashion Trends of the Early 2000s
articles.dek: From BAPE hoodies to Von Dutch hats to even the most tragic of fashion trends like unnecessary scarves, here are the best 2000s fashion trends you need to know
articles.author: Gregory Babcock
articles.text: Image via Getty/Evan Agostini This post was originally published in 2015. Nostalgia for the 2000s will likely reach an all time high as we go deeper into the 2020s. So close, yet so far away, the first decade of the 2000s were filled with a string of styles that were as iconic as the ‘80s and the ‘90s. Coming off the ‘90s, which at different points were both grungy and colorful, the rapid advancement of new technology brought a variety of sartorial influences for us to wear throughout the decade.Even today, we see artists co-sign clothing brands like Josué Thomas’ Gallery Dept. that have 2000s-era aesthetics, or brands like Palace leaning into all-over-print styles in their current collections. Nowadays, when you open up Tik-Tok or Instagram you’ll find plenty of young influencers dressing in “Y2K”-inspired styles. Accessories like mesh trucker caps and G-Shock watches are even coming back into fashion today. While it seems like fedoras and shutter shades have likely disappeared from vogue for good, it wouldn’t be too surprising to see them on everyone again a couple years from now. Everything in fashion just moves in circles. But for every fire retro fit you had (which naturally matched yourcoveted sneakers), there were plenty of dudes hitting the streets in bootcut jeans, oxford shoes, and an Ed Hardy V-neck. But even the most tragic of fashion trends of the time left its impact on men’s closets—even if that impact is reminding guys on what not to add to their wardrobes. And despite hindsight being 20/20, we still have to recognize that most of these styles felt hard in the moment—as is the case with most trends—which is all that matters when you’re trying to get a fit off. From the all-over BAPE hoodies to the rise and fall of the Von Dutch trucker hat, these are The 25 Best Trends of the early 2000s. Rapper Clothing Brands For every Sean Jean, and Rocawear; there was an Akoo, Nostic, and Vokal. Throughout the 2000’s, if a rapper had a little bit of money and was willing to attach his name to a brand, he’d send out a clothing line. While most of these 2000s Hip Hop fashion brands ended up at your local T.J. Maxx and A.J, Wright (R.I.P.), this trend would evolve into some impressive, critically appreciated collections—like Andre 3000’s Benjamin Bixby. While rapper clothing lines have evolved into things like Kanye West’s Yeezy Season 1 and 2, it’s safe to say that attempts at rapper-related clothing are mixed at best. Sweatbands Whether you were coming from the court, or were cutting your wrists, sweatbands had bizarre crossover appeal. In hip-hop, they were like batters’ gloves in the '90s, a bizarre sports accessory that dudes started rocking in completely non-athletic contexts. In punk and emo circles, they had the same effect—ultimately becoming an accessory that was as ubiquitous as your local mall's Hot Topic. Today they're relegated back to exclusive wear during the sports that inspired the trend, but we'll lament their role as the most athletic way to show you're unathletic. Streaky Hair Highlights Your sister's favorite boy band had them. Your auntie had them. A friend had them. For a minute, you definitely considered adding some extra light into your hairstyle. Sure, in retrospect, the style looked obnoxious at best (and like a skunk at worst), but back in the early-aughts it was the way to look like you hair was sun-kissed...whatever that means. Tall Tees So cheap you could buy several for a dollar, but functional and simple enough to go with basically anything, the tall tee was one of hip hop's most visible trends in the 2000s. Sure, it was hit with controversy—mostly with people who saw the T-shirt as a sign of drug dealers and African American stereotypes come to life. Tall tees were banned in clubs, condemned in the press, and used as a tool to profile individuals. But at the end of the day, isn't it just a t-shirt that's four sizes too big? Trucker Hats When Ashton Kutcher and Britney Spears wore their Von Dutch trucker hats, they set off a headwear revolution. As the name implies, they get their name from the big rig drivers who wore (and were most likely given) the meshed hat on their long drives. It was one of the many “ironic” fashion staples of the decade, and something that would gradually fade out as the joke of dressing like Hank Hill or Fall Out Boy's Patrick Stump wore off. Livestrong Bracelets Don’t lie, you had one of these on your wrist. If it wasn’t the iconic yellow, everyone had at least one of these rubber bracelets wrapped around their wrists during the last decade. Nothing makes people feel like they’re making a difference to a well-known cause like copping a bracelet and wearing it everywhere—it’s one of the key philosophies of the new millennium, right? Either way, once anyone and everyone began making these for just about anything under the sun, they quickly faded out of favor (Lance Armstrong’s cheating revelations certainly didn’t help either). Popped Collar Polos Preppy style has been a staple regardless of decade. Who doesn't like to exude privilege and wealth at every possible moment? With the rise and dominance of teen retailers like Abercrombie & Fitch and Hollister, their brand of prep Americana was in every mall (and at every cool kids' table) during the first half of the '00s. Around the time Kanye West dropped his first album in 2004, you probably remember catching him on TRL (R.I.P.) with his prepped out style, even popping his own collar on the cover his Freshman Adjustment mixtape. Hey, if 2000s hip-hop heavyweights Three 6 Mafia can name one of the biggest hit songs of the decade after popping your collar, then there's definitely something to this aughts-era trend. All-Over Prints Shouts to Bape (and the pursuing copycats) for this one. Aside from the full-zip hoodies, Bape and Billionaire Boys Club helped to front the all over prints onto everything from T-shirts to hats. Generally involving a repeating icon or graphic, coupled with an arrangement of pastel colors, these are the types of pieces that made sure everyone knew your personal style from at least two miles away. Whether you were a fan of “Dipset Anthem,” or just were really into The Neptunes, it's more likely than not that you had something that was completely covered in print. V-Neck T-shirts Yes, only the bravest of men would dive deep into the deep-V-neck game, but we'd be fronting if we didn't call out this as a trend. As retailers like American Apparel became more ubiquitous, the T-shirt crossed the country, overtaking the crewneck shirt as the de facto garb of hipsters and mall shoppers alike. While a V-neck's original purpose is to operate as undershirt, the piece quickly became as commonplace as the graphic tee of the 1990s. But by the end of the decade, there were more people making fun of the V-neck tee than there were people wearing it. Hoodies Under Blazers Straight out of the closets of John Legend-wannabes , this is a reminder that sometimes, you really can't dress down formalwear. A sign of a dude who really couldn't make up his mind, it was a combination of the casual and formal; a predecessor to the modern layering games of today. Mostly worn by dudes who looked like Common in the mid-00s, it's like dudes who wear denim, a sportscoat and dress shoes. You end up looking like a dad at best or end up as the subject of a Kanye West rant at worst. Bowties Geek chic is an invention of the 2000s. As traditionally nerdy pursuits and topics hit the mainstream (thanks Internet and rapid technological development), so did the desire of looking like Steve Urkel. The common move was to wear a bowtie with a J.Crew dress shirt tucked into jeans. Bonus points if suspenders made an appearance as well. As prep made a resurgence in the latter-half of the decade, dudes really thought they could make the look work in daily life. Sadly, with the rise of Sprezzatura roughly around the same time, most dudes just looked like professors at a southern university. Cardigans Remember how we talked on about the bizarre fusion of influences that created the “geek chic” trend? While the 2000s saw a rise in suburbanites shopping in thrift stores, it became ever more popular to dress like your grandpa. From the end of emo music's effect on the mainstream, into the rise of hipster culture at the end of the 2000s, cardigans made your grandparents one of the most relevant style icons. And don't lie, you know you wanted a Comme des Garçons PLAY cardigan with the heart. Big Face Digital Watches The 1980s really were in full revival during the new millennium. What better way to pay homage to the decade than with a giant Casio or G-Shock? Maybe it had to do with all of the Flavor-Flav on VH1 during the decade, but the bigger the watch face the better when it came to your timepiece. Retro-meets-modern, and usually in a loud-as-hell colorway, these were the watches to rock if you didn't make a ton of cash, but still wanted to stunt. Shutter Shades We're certain that Kanye didn't know what he started when he got the ball rolling on shutter shades. Obliviously stemming from West's unstoppable album, Graduation, shutter shades became the de facto pointless accessory; someone would be caught wearing a pair in literally any and every public place—from senior prom, to the New Jersey boardwalk. Part of the 80's revival of the late 2000s, the shutter shades are actually a piece that came out of archives of eyewear designer Alain Mikli. Fortunately, due to the cyclical nature of fashion (or the fact that you genuinely cannot see where you're going wearing a pair of these), they faded out by the time Ye went into hiding post-2009 VMAs. Graffiti-Inspired Urban Wear Airbrushed tees were a product of the '80s, but the 2000s drew inspiration from the street’s biggest artists. Brands like Ecko Unltd., Fubu, and PNB Nation, all incorporated spraypaint and street art into their clothing in same fashion or another. Ecko even had his own branded video game centered around being a graffiti artist. Even Shepard Fairey's Obey made its mark near the end of decade thanks in part to his iconic “Hope” portrait of Barack Obama. Throwback Jerseys Mitchell & Ness made a killing outfitting dudes in retro jerseys and fitteds, reviving old school logos in such a big way that by the time Allen Iverson was dominating the NBA, it was nearly impossible not to see him without something retro related. Yes, the style became way too oversaturated way too quickly, but there's no denying the fact that this trend helped spawn the customizer movement we see today via Don C and Eric Emanuel. Bootcut Jeans We doubt that more dudes were wearing boots at the turn of the century, but for some reason, the bootcut jean saw an immense swell in availability in the 2000s. Fitted like a straight leg jean but with a wider opening at the base. If you think of them like the menswear answer to the ladies’ “flare” jeans, then you wouldn't be too far off. While they do have their purpose—mainly to accommodate wearing high rise boots—the practical nature of straight leg jeans overrides the need for jeans with an OD leg opening. Matching Outfit to Sneakers Getting ready was a process in the 2000s. While most guys today compliment their footwear to their outfit, it’s safe to say that most dudes aren't making sure that their sneakers replicate the exact colors of their head-to-toe kit. Spurred on by more outlandish colorways and a burgeoning sneakerhead scene, guys wouldn't just hunt for classic colorways of their favorite sneakers on release day—they'd be buying sneakers to match clothes in their closet. Of course, this meant nothing if you didn't have the the hat to match, natch. Tattoo-Inspired Brands The choice of VH1 reality show stars and celebrity parents alike, these brands ran amok in the mid-aughts. You're likely familiar with the chief offenders; a combination of Ed Hardy, Affliction, and Xtreme Couture plastered their over-the-top tattoo inspired designs on nearly every D-list celeb from Hollywood to the Jersey Shore (literally). If a child star or ex-boy band/girl group were still clinging to relevancy, it's likely they would be doing so clad in one of these brands. Unnecessary Scarves You know when you see someone wearing a scarf in the summertime or inside a well-heated building? You can blame the 2000s for that one. Keffiyehs or circle scarves, there's little question that the rise of hipster culture is the genesis of this temperature defying trend. Like a necklace, the most common way to wear this style would be with a simple T-shirt and skinny jeans. While this was certainly more rampant during the '00s, in no way has this trend died out. One trip to a Brooklyn dive bar with live music, and you'll stumble across this at some point. Writte by GREGORY BABCOCK

articles.title: Virgil Abloh: The Designer of Progress
articles.author: Luke Leitch
articles.text: Virgil Abloh, who has died today aged 41, will be remembered as one of the most popular and influential fashion designers of his era. As both the founder of Off-White and the Creative Director of Menswear for Louis Vuitton, Abloh’s ascent from show-crashing fashion tourist in 2009 to the very apex of the global luxury industry at the time of his passing is arguably the defining fashion story of the 2010s. For as both an African American and a creative whose work emerged from the rag-tag genre of streetwear—a genre whose definition he regularly contested—Abloh was the seminal boundary breaker in a notoriously bordered business. Abloh’s influence, however, will also be remembered well beyond fashion. It was only six months ago that he observed in an interview: “I operate by my own rules, in my own logic, and I’m not fearful.” By 2021 that same unorthodox process that fueled his unprecedented rise in a world so often ruled by convention had led him to see his fashion design as only the by-product of a greater end. This was, as he described it, “making a global community regardless of the elitism or sort of territorial-ness that can happen in subculture.” Abloh’s greatest product of all was the varied creation of opportunity for others to whom opportunity is otherwise routinely denied. In 2017, for instance, he created a uniform for Melting Passes, a team of recently immigrated soccer players in Paris whose lack of residency status meant they were excluded from playing in official competition, and later included them in the audience at an Off-White show. There were 3,000 students at his first Louis Vuitton show at the Palais Royal gardens in 2018. He worked to support skateboarders and surfers in Ghana, the birth-country of his parents, and provided funds to fix park and play facilities in Chicago, the city he called home. Photo: Acielle / Style du Monde Virgil Abloh backstage at his fall 2018 Off-White show. Photographed by Corey Tenold He added: “And that’s why I focus on design, while I’m also focusing on asking what and who can I shine a light on. You know it’s not just about making art or fashion for its own sake: there are kids in Accra who can become attached and engaged in the skateboarding community if someone builds a bridge. And there are kids in the South Side of Chicago that need education and health: how does what I’m doing tie into that? What’s the bridge for that? That’s sort of the ethos of my career. You know, I started the Post-Modern Scholarship Fund and raised a million dollars to offer assistance in the education of black students. Those things, they’re critical to me.” Most recently, in July, that critical imperative in Abloh’s thinking received the backing of LVMH, which announced that he would consult for the conglomerate at an executive level, acting to create positive disruption across the group. Virgil Abloh was born in 1980 in Rockford, Illinois, to Nee and Eunice Abloh, who had emigrated to the United States from Ghana. When not at school Abloh developed an early passion for skateboarding—which he credited with sparking his first interest in fashion—and later DJing, which would become another key facet in his lifetime's work. While studying Civil Engineering at the University of Wisconsin and later the Illinois Institute of Technology he encountered Kanye West, another unorthodox thinker, who was so impressed that he installed Abloh as his ‘creative director’ in 2002. During the next few years Abloh’s many activities included launching a retail space gallery, working in the Been Trill collective alongside Heron Preston and Matthew Williams, and launching Pyrex Vision, a now long-defunct brand that is still bootlegged to this day. In 2009 he made his most personally significant launch of all: a successful proposal of marriage to his then girlfriend of a decade, Shannon Sundberg. Virgil Abloh (far right), with Kanye West and friends, in Paris. Photographed by Tommy Ton in January 2009 outside of the Comme des Garçons fall 2009 show. That was also the year that, now famously, Abloh joined West and their associates Don C, Taz Arnold, Chris Julian, and Fonzworth Bentley to attend the Paris fashion shows: West later estimated they managed to gain access to just over half of them. In the same year, Abloh joined West for an internship at the Fendi headquarters in Rome, and the year after joined West’s Donda project. By 2013 the designer decided to pivot from Pyrex Vision in order to focus on a fresh concept he’d named Off-White. He shared this idea with County of Milan’s Marcelo Burlon, a fellow spirit, designer, and DJ, who encouraged Abloh to manufacture Off-White through what would later become the New Guards group in Milan. Virgil Abloh with Naomi Campbell at the close of his spring 2018 Off-White show. The reveal of the first Off-White collection in 2014 coincided with a broader shift in the currents of fashion. Responding, at first slowly, to shifting consumer desires that proved difficult to rationalize against established luxury clothing categories, houses had started tentatively offering sneakers. But a generation that habitually wore sneakers and rarely considered tailoring increasingly demanded more—they wanted ‘streetwear.’ By showing pure streetwear in a fashion show context Abloh’s Off-White breached the dam between fashion’s ivory tower and the street’s more inverted forms of sneakerhead discernment. In 2015 Off-White was nominated for the LVMH Prize and by 2018, when greater seismic shifts in the menswear sector led to a four-house creative reshuffle, Abloh was championed by Kim Jones to take over the job at Louis Vuitton. Alongside Olivier Rousteing at Balmain, he duly became only one of two Black designers in the leading design role at a Parisian house. That sunny afternoon show on June 21, 2018, was held on a rainbow runway and distinctly felt like a watershed moment in fashion—which it was. After he took his bow, Abloh and West exchanged an ecstatic hug. As Vogue Runway reported: “The last look was a metallic silver poncho with “Follow the Yellow Brick'' written on a breast patch. When he posted a picture of that moment on his Instagram, the caption read, “You can do it too.” Virgil Abloh was born September 30, 1980, and died on November 28, 2021. He is survived by his wife Shannon, and children Lowe, 8, and Grey, 5 as well as his parents Nee and Eunice and sister Edwina. articles.title: The Origins of Billionaire Boys Club/Icecream, Pharrell and NIGO's Brainchild
