articles.title: Dominatrixes photographed on their own terms
articles.dek: A Body of Mirrors is a powerful new exhibition which presents an insider’s portrait of BDSM and the women who practice it
articles.author: Phoebe Hennell
articles.text: Hannah Louise, A Body of Mirrors Through photographing seven professional dominatrixes, Louise challenges the rigid archetype of a severe, feminine woman dressed as a secretary. She discovered that “pro dommes are world-builders, artists, healers and weirdos who facilitate incredible spaces for self-discovery, expansion and release”. They do not break character, denying the viewer the chance to fully know them. By capturing her subjects from below, snarling, or sitting on someone’s face, the photos assume the gaze of the submissive, preserving the psychological dynamic which characterises BDSM. The power gaps and elements of ambiguity “invite projection, and projection is always revealing,” explains the show’s curator, Barbara Kaczmarczyk. “By resisting the fantasy of complete access, it perhaps makes the viewer aware of their own assumptions.” This projection is precisely where A Body of Mirrors gets its name. “The submissive looks at the domme and finds their own reflection warped across her body,” says Kaczmarczyk. Latex is explored as a symbolic mirror. People come to dominatrixes with their fantasies, but rarely receive them back unchanged – the domme interprets them, redirects them and sometimes even turns them against the sub. “Similarly, latex reflects everything around it, but returns a distorted image.” Mistress Nalini Westwood & Caspian, London, 2026 Photography Hannah Louise A professional domme herself, Louise wields a camera with an insider perspective that intersects with her art. This allows her to go beyond “static fetish portraits” and capture the full scope of these characters. Existing within the same marginalised community as her subjects gives an immediate, unspoken baseline of understanding, Louise has found. “I know how it feels to be photographed by someone who just sees a ‘hot woman’ in an outfit, versus through the eyes of someone who truly shares your vision of beauty and power.” Kaczmarczyk, also a pro domme, adds that their practice as dominatrixes enabled them to skip the usual routine of defending or explaining sex workers, and to author their own narratives. “I could take all that as given and treat our work as a cultural practice, rather than a social problem,” they say. From the brothels in Fanny Hill to season three of Euphoria, stories about sex workers are overwhelmingly told by outsiders – meanwhile, digital platforms shadowban actual sex workers. The iconography, too, is lifted by the fashion industry – once the reserve of fetishwear shops, latex and body stockings saturate the runways, while Pleaser-style stripper heels are worn far from any pole. “Mainstream culture mines sex worker aesthetics,” says Louise. “Yet the marginalised people responsible for giving those garments their edge and cultural capital face intense stigma.” In this era of stifling censorship on the one hand and appropriation on the other, A Body of Mirrors, and the ethos of self-authored representation at its core, is an important intervention. A Body of Mirrors runs at Stuck (32–36 Tottenham Road, London N1 4WD) until 19 August 2026.

articles.title: Kembra Pfahler's guide to becoming an artist
articles.dek: Subversive performance artist Kembra Pfahler shares advice for aspiring artists on her DIY philosophy, embracing being hated and stepping out from behind our screens
articles.author: Laura Pitcher
articles.text: When legendary rockstar and performance artist Kembra Pfahler walks into a room – these days, often wearing a balaclava, sunglasses and dark lipstick – people take notice. Few artists have commanded such a lasting legacy. As a key figure in the Lower East Side’s underground scene, Pfahler’s performances have influenced New York culture for more than four decades. On stage, Pfahler, who is the high priestess of The Voluptuous Horror of Karen Black, became known for getting naked and covering herself in head-to-toe single-colour body paint (even blacking out her teeth), wearing her signature three-tiered black wig and stiletto boots. Who better, then, to teach a performance art 101 class? In late July, I woke up bright and early to head to Art Omi in Ghent, New York, for exactly that. Pfahler arrived at the not-for-profit arts centre and 120-acre sculpture and architecture park in a green jumpsuit, ringing a large gnome-shaped bell to say that class is in session. On a whiteboard, she wrote the word “AVAILABISM” in big letters – an artistic practice she came up with centred on making use of what is readily available. On stage, availabism can look like showing up with a large cut-out sheet wrapped around you, rather than any expensive stage clothes, but the philosophy also extends to every corner of life. For example, during introductions, when someone mentioned they were shy, Pfahler told them to “hold onto” their shyness. “Being shy is a good thing,” she said, before explaining how she’s less inclined to work with people who crave the spotlight. Availabism, then, in that context, is about leaning into what comes naturally to you. “You don’t have to be the performer; you could be the director, you could be the costume maker, or you could be the person that’s filming your friend,” Pfahler told me when I caught up with her after class. Perhaps even more impressive than Pfahler’s fierce and wild performances over the years – all documented in her new Rizzoli book, which she says she worked with senior editor Loren Olsen on for about 7 years – is her commitment to shape the next generation of artists. “My desire has always been to create things from nothing,” she says. And Pfahler is a natural teacher. She invited everyone to join her on stage at her next show, and put her number on the whiteboard at the end of class – when she said to call her “anytime”, she actually meant it. Below, we asked her for her takeaways from decades of availabism, in her own words. Courtesy of Art Omi “I’M AN AVAILABIST, I MAKE THE BEST USE OF WHAT’S AVAILABLE” That’s the sentence that started it all – Pfahler recounts saying it to her teacher, artist Joseph Kosuth, at the School of Visual Arts, when he asked her what she was. “I took great offence because I didn’t know what I was when I was a 17-year-old,” she says. Shortly after, she quit school. Thankfully, she found her community in New York “right away”. Shortly after moving to New York, she organised “The Extremist Show”, a nine-day event that mixed performance and music with drawings, paintings, and sculpture at ABC No Rio arts space. “ABC No Rio has been given to the younger generation to take over as a free space to use and curate shows,” she says. “I was very fortunate because I found that in New York – not only did I have this idea, but I had a community of people to help me understand what I was doing.” According to Pfahler, it took her another decade to understand “what it meant”. “WE WERE THE DEVALUED CLOWNS OF THE ART WORLD” When Pfahler was just getting started, she says performance art was not taken seriously and performance people were “the devalued clowns of the art world”. This, of course, didn’t stop her from creating her own subversive visual language, exploring themes of horror, sex and feminism. In the 1980s, Pfahler funded her underground film projects with work at an independent porn studio. She says she was “angry” when she first started, but encourages emerging artist to think “very seriously” about using their nakedness in public. “You always have to be prepared to talk about your performance at the dinner table with your grandmother at a Jewish, Buddhist or Muslim holiday,” she says. “It’s impossible to do things in secret.” This, says Pfahler, was a lesson she learned especially during her more extreme performances, like when she sewed her vagina shut for Richard Kern’s Sewing Circle (1992), and then had to explain that to her 11-year-old nephew at the time. “I never thought that being naked was sexual because it wasn’t about adult sexuality,” she says. “It was about beauty, power and not having – coming from extreme body shame and dysmorphia.” Throughout the 1990s, Pfahler continued to explore how physical transformations could challenge conventions around aesthetics, gender and performance art, including in her performances in The Voluptuous Horror of Karen Black. Courtesy of Art Omi “DON’T DO A PERFORMANCE BECAUSE YOU WANT TO GO STRAIGHT TO THE TOP” Pfahler says she always suggests people don’t do a performance just because they want the accolades. “You’re doing a performance to share new ideas,” she says. “I think I learned from the punk generation in the early 70s in Los Angeles that you are going to give yourself a nervous breakdown if every time you do something, you want to go straight to the top.” In fact, in the beginning, people in America didn’t understand The Voluptuous Horror of Karen Black. This didn’t deter them from doing a cross-country tour in the 90s anyway. “I never toured in Europe with my band because Europeans always treated New Yorkers so openly and positively,” she says. “I thought to myself, ‘I have to tour in the US where they hate my guts because they don’t have anything like us’.” This was before Marilyn Manson rose to popularity, and Pfahler says New Yorkers would say they were “homosexual heroin addicts” who wore too much makeup. The entire purpose for touring in places where you didn’t receive a warm welcome, according to Pfahler, was that they’d end up playing in cities where there were “three punk rock gay kids” who would always be waiting for them during soundcheck. “WE DON’T KNOW WHO IS GOING TO SAVE THE WORLD OR CHANGE THE WORLD. I THINK ALL OF US DO IN OUR OWN LITTLE WAYS JUST BY SHOWING UP” Pfahler developed a couple of hard rules over her years of experimental performance. One is to always pay people. The other is to do no harm (including to herself). “In the beginning, I used house paints that put me in the hospital and glitter made of glass that can cut your eyes,” she says. “I had to learn the hard way about materials. A breakthrough came to her during a conversation with Sharon Stone, who said something along the lines of “We all have to be careful”. “I was like, ‘Jesus Christ, you’re absolutely right’.” Other than those simple rules, Pfahler encourages everyone to experience the freedom of embarrassing themselves in public. “We don’t know who is going to save the world or change the world,” she says. “I think all of us do in our own little ways just by showing up.” With this in mind, Pfahler says it’s never too late to start a band or schedule a solo performance – which she recommends just picking a date for, making a flyer and then “figuring it all out later”. Availabism includes inventing performance spaces out of nowhere and having the courage to ask questions like, “What are you doing with all this fabric after your wedding?”. During the performance 101 class, Pfahler emphasised the importance of reaching out to artists you admire and doing studio visits. Or, as she put it, “pursuing people who are alive”. In an age where it’s easy to hide behind a screen, it’s sobering advice. “Availabism can be confusing if there’s an excess of apligants [Pfahler’s made-up word for application-driven intelligence], but if you ask AI how to build a lemonade stand, it‘s going to give you 50 thousand different ways to build it, and that can be confusing,” she says. “The internet is a handful of rich white guys’ opinions”.

articles.title: Young people are foraging their way out of the cost-of-living crisis
articles.author: Ali Pantony
articles.text: The age-old practice of foraging for food has become an escape from the hell of modern life and a source of free ingredients – birch twig biscuit, anyone? It’s a sun-drenched afternoon in south London, and I’m surrounded by food. No, I’m not in a supermarket or restaurant, and I haven’t just loaded up on picky bits for a park picnic. I’m in the Rookery, a community-run garden on the southern edge of Streatham Common, but if you were to see the abundant nature around me – branches peppered with olives, creeping tomato vines bursting with ripe, juicy fruits and towering cherry trees against a cloudless blue sky – you’d think I was somewhere far more exotic than SW16. “There’s rosemary here, chard, elderberries, chamomile, liquorice mint,” says Rebekah Williams, a 29-year-old British-Jamaican herbalist and environmental educator who is leading me on a foraging walk around the common. “At this time of year, all the plants are starting to seed, so it’s a great time to gather nettle seeds which help with energy levels and vitality.” Williams is the founder of Earth Child Remedies, a community-centred wellness initiative that helps to reconnect global majority and queer communities back to the land. She’s been leading foraging walks around the country since 2023, but has seen a noticeable rise in young people taking up the hobby in the last year. “There seems to be a recent awakening to the fact that modern life – working 9-5 jobs, only getting 20 days’ holiday a year, spending more time indoors staring at a screen than outdoors – really isn’t good for us,” she says. “I think people are turning to foraging because they’re realising how disconnected we’ve become from the land.” It wasn’t always this way. Around 250,000 years ago, people were predominantly nomadic hunter-gatherers who relied on the land and changing ecological systems for food and medicine. The gradual shift from foraging to farming started with the Neolithic Revolution 12,000 years ago, then the Industrial Revolution, which allowed for large-scale food production. The 20th century transformed the global food system through refrigeration, processing and international trade. Today, we mostly rely on supermarket chains and large-scale corporate farming for our food, but the pandemic, various global conflicts and extreme weather have exposed just how fragile the supply chains underpinning that system can be. For most of us, the idea of snacking on a wild-growing plant or fungus is still a little disconcerting. But this is starting to change. On TikTok, there are over 3,000 posts of UK foragers making everything from linden seed chocolate to wild garlic and oyster mushroom toast. Foraging has become a viral niche for nature content creators, from Sussex-based Fern Freud (@foragedbyfern) who has amassed 185,000 followers sharing wild-food recipes and foraging tips, to Megan Howlett of @theforagerscottage, who has built a following of over 277,000 from posting foraged-ingredient recipes including pineapple weed and water pepper sauerkraut; birch twig biscuits and lavender oat lattes. Searches for ‘foraging’ are also up by a third on Google since last year, and Waitrose has seen a surge in customers searching for recipes for foraged ingredients. For many young people, foraging has become an indispensable mindfulness practice. “For me, it’s about having a connection with the seasons and the living world,” says 27-year-old Elsa Evelyn. “ When I’m foraging, I can feel my restless mind quieting, and it’s the only time I walk slowly because I’m spying for edible opportunities. I love this time because it feels like a conversation between myself and the earth.” Originally from Winchester, where she’d scour the hedgerows for rosehips, sloes and hawthorn berries, Evelyn moved to Devon last year and says the foraging opportunities have multiplied. “Bilberries, or wild English blueberries, grow abundantly across Dartmoor, alongside pennywort and horsetail. Last week, I picked cherry plums and early-season blackberries and added them to a pavlova.” Similarly, for 28-year-old Amy Sarah, foraging in Hampshire is about connecting with the planet – and protecting it. “I started picking wild berries in my local wild park and storing them in the freezer, mainly because I wanted to cut down my plastic consumption from supermarkets. Eating directly from the earth is not only nutrient-dense and delicious, but a powerful way to ground us in gratitude for plants that so many people walk past. It's another layer of connection with the planet, and a practice of presence and mindfulness.” As my trip to Streatham with Williams confirms, foraging isn’t solely reserved for those in rural communities. In fact, foraging and wild food tours are cropping up across the UK’s urban areas, from seaweed, sorrel and samphire foraging along Kent’s coastal towns, to foliage and fungi in Sheffield, wild pizza workshops in Leeds and even foraged cocktail classes in Mile End. Divya Hariramani Herrero runs Fruity Walks, fruit-picking and -spotting expeditions for like-minded young people across London. “I set it up in 2020 during the pandemic because I found the most perfect pear tree growing in my local park, St James’ Churchyard in Bermondsey. I come from Madrid, and I just didn’t realise any fruit would grow in London. My mind was completely blown. I thought, ‘Everybody needs to know about this’.” Herrero started an Instagram showcasing the fruit trees she’d spotted around the city, including apple trees, plum trees, grapefruits, pomegranates, lemons, loquats, persimmons, and even a 12-metre avocado tree behind Tate Modern. Some of these trees are on private land and reflect London’s multicultural heritage. “I started knocking on people’s doors and realised these trees had been planted by people from all over the world, from the Windrush Generation, Grenada, Jamaica, St Lucia, Bangladesh, Cyprus and Turkey who wanted to plant something familiar to them.” Herrero started running fruit-spotting walks for her followers and telling them the stories behind the people who planted them, but this quickly turned into fruit-picking walks for trees on public land. So far, she’s taken over a thousand people on walks. “I think it’s because we’re so plugged into our laptops, AI, social media – people just want to get out and connect with nature and experience their cities differently.” I ask Williams if she thinks the rising cost of living has anything to do with increased interest in foraging. “Absolutely, because foraging can really help you in times when you have less money,” she says. “You can forage some nettles, three-cornered leek and garlic, and at least make a meal for yourself. You could also gather medicinal plants like elderberries, freeze them, and make them into a syrup to ward off colds in the winter, saving money on going to the pharmacy.” But like every keen forager I speak to, Williams is keen to highlight the importance of doing so responsibly. “Never take more than you need,” she advises. “You only need a small amount to make a cup of tea, and if there’s not much, leave it alone. Bees, birds, insects and other living organisms also rely on the plants for shelter, food and medicine. So if we approach foraging from a capitalistic perspective of extraction, then all we’re going to do is deplete it.” Ben McCarthy, Head of Nature Conservation at the National Trust, adds that while foraging can be good fun and help people connect with nature, “excessive foraging, or foraging on protected sites, can be detrimental” to wildlife and negatively impact delicate ecosystems. He asks that foragers follow the code of conduct and countryside code: “respect, protect and enjoy.” As my trip with Rebekah comes to an end, I tell her I’m genuinely surprised by how relaxed I feel, like someone’s flicked a switch in my nervous system. “I hear that all the time,” she says, smiling. “For me, foraging is like my meditation. It really helped me after the pandemic when my mental health was really not in a good place. Foraging is really what brought me out of that time. I owe a lot to this practice.”

articles.title: Your London Fashion Week SS27 cheat sheet is here!
articles.dek: From McQueen’s dramatic return to a new slate of up-and-coming talent, here’s everything you need to know about SS27 season this September
articles.author: Isobel Van Dyke
articles.text: Our tans are fading and we’ve stopped finding sand in every crevice. Just as we’ve broken in our flip-flops, it’s time to put them away again. As we near the end of August, most of the population will be thinking about going back to work and school. But for those working in fashion, a mammoth SS27 ready-to-wear season awaits. As usual, things kick off in the Big Apple on September 10, before heading to London the following week. And there’s a lot going on. Between the grand returns, the debuts and the off-schedule secret plans (watch this space for the lowdown on those), there’s a lot of information to brush-up on. Allow us to assist… THE NEW KIDS ON THE BLOCK Petra Fagerström AW26 There’s a whole host of new faces this season. After making her on-schedule debut in February, Swedish designer Petra Fagerström is set to host her debut runway show. Alongside her will be fellow CSM graduate, Portuguese designer Gui Rosa, who becomes the latest talent to join the NEWGEN cohort. After joining NEWGEN last summer, Liza Keane will be one to watch – we’ve been fans since 2023 (as has Julia Fox) and all eyes will be on her upcoming debut catwalk show. Antonio Vattev's label, av vattev, known for its whimsical cardigans, can also be spotted on schedule for the first time. The Bulgarian designer will host a screening on Sunday afternoon. Aletta was reborn as A Letter at the start of 2026, meaning that technically, come September, the brand is set to make its runway debut under the new name. It’ll also be a first for Leeds university menswear graduate Geordie Campbell, who caught the industry’s attention earlier this summer with his ‘Queer Boy’ graphic tees. THE RETURNING RISING STARS Oscar Ouyang SS26 E.W.USIE will be hosting appointments across the weekend, meanwhile Saul Nash will be curating a three-day pop-up. Of course, everyone will also be interested to see how Tolu Coker tops her last show, during which the king made a surprise entrance. THE SEPTEMBER LOYALISTS Chopova Lowena SS26 Of the various fashion weeks that happen around the world and throughout the year, September’s ready-to-wear season is by far the biggest. With the rising costs of putting on a fashion show, several independent London brands prefer to show once a year, skipping the February shows in favour of September. These include brands like Ahluwalia, Chopova Lowena and Aaron Esh, meanwhile KNWLS returns to the London Fashion Week schedule following a two-year hiatus, during which it made its Milan debut. THE HOT TICKETS Photography Robin Galiegue Historically, Burberry has been the biggest name on the LFW schedule. But this season, it’s got competition. It was announced earlier this year that McQueen would make its grand return to London after 25 years of showing in Paris. Undoubtedly, the brand will bring its supermodel casting and celebrity front row with it. Elsewhere, Christopher Kane is due to make his debut as creative director of Mulberry, which will be another major moment. A MOMENT FOR THE JEWELLERY The London jewellery scene has been slowly carving out a space for itself on the LFW schedule. Of the current NEWGEN line-up, two of the designers are exciting independent jewellers, OCTI and The Ouze. Plus, Dover Street Market will once again host its seasonal jewellery showcase, in which it celebrates emerging jewellery designers. If you thought fashion week was all about the clothes, you thought wrong!

articles.title: How to date when... you're afraid to say how you really feel
articles.dek: Afraid that speaking your mind or sharing your emotions will scare people away? Here, Beth McColl shares her advice for opening up when dating someone new
articles.author: Beth McColl
articles.text: In Partnership with Hinge I haven’t always been on the most familiar terms with my feelings. I knew about them, of course- but in a vague, distant relative-y type of way. They were cousins that I didn’t like much. Uncles that I hoped not to see at family dos. Nieces that I- well, you get the picture. When it came to matters of love and dating, I thought of my feelings as complicating little distractions, and so I shunned them. There were entire relationships where I barely told myself how I felt, let alone the person I was with. My thesis was this: I would secure love by being easy-going and cool, by pretending I wasn’t [insert so-called “negative” emotion] when I absolutely was [insert so-called “negative” emotion] and by filing away my true needs and wants in a brain-drawer labelled Absolutely Confidential. Anyway, it obviously didn’t work. Whether I liked it or not, my feelings weren’t there to piss me off or make problems. It took several entanglements falling apart in the most frustrating ways and one serious relationship ending after months of me trying to force my feelings of dissatisfaction into submission, but eventually I had to come home to a new way of seeing my emotions. They were just messengers – delivering inarguable and non-negotiable information about my wants, needs, values, desires and opinions. So, all there was to it was to learn how to open my mouth and make myself known. When you’re afraid to truly show up as yourself in words or actions, you can end up mirroring the person you’re dating – consciously or not. If they like going with the flow and hate talking about feelings, then you might pretend you’re the same way inclined, even if in reality that gives you a stomach ache and a splitting headache behind one eyeball. This isn’t real love at its best, nor is it a situation where love can really even get going. Eventually, the truth of who you are and what you’re feeling will arrive in full force. When you’re afraid to truly show up as yourself in words or actions, you can end up mirroring the person you’re dating – consciously or not. Eventually, the truth of who you are and what you’re feeling will arrive in full force In the past I’ve struggled to open up about difficult moments from my dating history, my mental illness, my abandonment fears. But I’ve also struggled to say smaller and sweeter truths, too. “I like you” and “this is really fun” and “I can see a future here”. It’s only now, from the hard-won vantage point of a loving relationship, that I can see what I was costing myself each time I held back. A chance to be truly known, to build a relationship around my needs, to offer my true feelings up like a gift to the person that had made them happen. As with so many things, it’s a good idea to take this slow until you feel more at home in the idea and more able to trust your instincts. Start small. If your knee-jerk reaction is to play down your emotions when put on the spot, then practice telling the person you’re with that you need some time and space to think before you share. You can then use that time to organise your feelings on paper, or in a Word doc or talk about them to someone you trust who you know is a practised feelings-sayer. You can also start by taking smaller, more controlled risks and opening up little by little, emotional inch by emotional inch. This could look like sharing an honest opinion of the film you just watched, or the experimental flaming trout and vodka cocktail you ordered at the bar after. This is a low-stakes way to practice expressing what you really think and feel instead of what you think they want to hear. Tune back into your own tastes and opinions and remind yourself that disagreement or difference of opinion doesn’t need to be a disaster. It’s also totally normal to worry that sharing your feelings will result in a rejection, that they’ll be too much or too odd or too hard to contend with. But in fact, this tends to only be the case for people who aren’t totally right for you anyway. How does that saying go? To be loved is to be known. Yeah – that! It’s also totally normal to worry that sharing your feelings will result in a rejection, that they’ll be too much or too odd or too hard to contend with. But in fact, this tends to only be the case for people who aren’t totally right for you anyway This isn’t to say that every single thought or feeling has to be shared. A great relationship isn’t a never-ending exchange of every doubt or difficult emotion or question that comes up throughout the day (you’d never get anything else done) - it’s knowing that when it is time to share, you’re not going to find yourself on the receiving end of shame or suppression. So be discerning, but also be brave. If something really is bothering you or there’s important information that you suspect the other person isn’t aware of, then that’s your sign to calmly bring it up. Remember too that having someone be willing to make time and space for your feelings isn’t a ’nice to have’ – it’s a necessity. They’re not doing you a favour; they’re just participating in the relationship. My current partner has been excellent at meeting me halfway in this kind of feeling-exchange. When I was finding the long-distance element of our relationship hard, we sat down and found a solution together. When my Seasonal Affective Disorder flared up over the winter, he stepped in to support me and then later, when I felt better, he told me how it had felt for him. Now at 33 – an age that feels both incredibly young and also a million miles from my first formative relationships – I’ve realised that there’s really nothing else for it but to make an effort to know your feelings and find ways to share them with others. Doing so can be scary, but it will also allow your genuine wants and needs to flourish and will let you cease performing as anyone other than yourself. Speaking from experience, there isn’t much that feels better.

articles.title: Who is 'Dirty Deeds'?
articles.author: Adrian Medina
articles.text: WHO THE F*CK IS DIRTY DEEDS? Separated by hundreds of miles but connected by an obsessive love of creation, DIRTY DEEDS is bringing producers, artists, designers, filmmakers, and dreamers together to build something entirely their own. Most music groups begin in the same room. DIRTY DEEDS began across Texas. Austin. Corpus Christi. Weslaco. San Antonio. Different cities, different backgrounds, and different creative disciplines—all connected through FaceTime calls that regularly last an entire day, files sent back and forth at impossible hours, and the shared belief that the right group of people can create something greater than any of them could make alone. Calling DIRTY DEEDS a music group would only describe part of what it is. It is a creative collective made up of music producers, recording artists, designers, filmmakers, and dreamers. Music may be at its center, but there is no hard boundary around what the group can become. A song can lead to a film. A film can inspire a visual world. A conversation can become a record, a campaign, or the beginning of an idea none of us fully understand yet. That openness is the entire point. At the center of the collective is Mercye Evans, known as @yourmercye, a producer whose relationship with sound feels almost impossible to explain. “Mercye Evans is the best music producer I have ever fucking met.” — Adrian Medina There is no exaggeration in that statement. Mercye understands how to place sounds together in ways I have never seen or heard anyone else accomplish. His music feels considered without feeling restrained. He hears relationships between sounds that most people would never think to connect, then somehow makes those combinations feel inevitable. Mercye is also a film fanatic and a genuine music nerd in the purest sense of the word. He does not simply know the biggest directors, musicians, genres, and cultural moments. He knows the histories underneath them—the obscure names, forgotten movements, niche subgenres, technical decisions, and strange details most people would never think to research. Whether the conversation is about a universally celebrated filmmaker or a musical scene that existed for five minutes in one specific place, Mercye probably knows what happened, who influenced it, and why it mattered. That knowledge gives him an unusually deep creative vocabulary. He does not approach music as disconnected sound. He understands atmosphere, pacing, emotion, references, and the worlds that can exist around a record. I believe Mercye has the potential to become huge. My role right now is to help him organize the flood of ideas, prepare the music for release, build the visual language around it, and give him the push he has needed to place the work in front of people. Talent like his should not remain hidden inside hard drives, private messages, and unfinished folders. It deserves to be heard. Then there is Caleb, known as @m3d13y, one of the most talented and genuinely unique people I have ever known. I met Caleb on Omegle in 2018. Out of every random person we could have been connected with, it turned out that he lived only a few hours away from me. What could have been a brief internet interaction became a friendship that has lasted for years—and eventually became one of the foundations of DIRTY DEEDS. When I first met him, Caleb was a high-school percussionist, a role he maintained throughout all four years of school. But he never allowed his education to stop at what he was taught in class. Over the years, I watched him push far beyond the boundaries of a normal high-school music program. He kept learning, experimenting, and developing until music seemed less like a subject he studied and more like a language he could speak fluently. He learned practically every instrument he could put his hands on. He developed an understanding of composition, notation, rhythm, structure, and theory. He can write music, perform intricate riffs, study how a piece works, and then approach it from an entirely different direction. And on top of everything else, @m3d13y has the voice of an angel. Introducing Caleb to Mercye felt natural. Their abilities were different but deeply compatible, and from that point forward, we became inseparable. The connection was not manufactured through networking, management, or an industry strategy. It came from people who genuinely enjoyed creating together and recognized something special in one another. While working remotely from Texas as a designer for Rolling Loud, I would often spend entire days on FaceTime with the group—sometimes close to 15 hours at a time. We would work independently, exchange ideas, play unfinished music, discuss films, design visuals, make jokes, revise concepts, and continue talking long after any normal workday should have ended. Lately, those digital sessions have begun turning into more frequent in-person meetings. We travel, meet in the same city, shoot videos, develop ideas, and finally bring into one room the energy that had been building across our screens. Every time we work together in person, the potential of DIRTY DEEDS becomes more tangible. Danny Boy, known as @cudi.xz, brings another essential dimension to the collective. Danny is an incredible producer with a natural ear for music. His chords are rich and groovy. His drums move. His melodies carry emotion without having to force it. Working alongside Mercye and Caleb, Danny has helped create some of the most beautiful music I have ever heard. Their strengths do not compete with one another—they multiply. One person may introduce a chord progression, another may hear the melody hiding inside it, and someone else may reshape the entire emotional direction of the record. The music becomes a conversation, with each person hearing something the others might have missed. DIRTY DEEDS is also currently creating with Montell, known as @RNBMSL, an artist we consider nothing short of a GOAT. Montell has a beautiful voice and a wide recording range that allows him to move between ideas without losing his identity. He knows how to become part of a record while still sounding unmistakably like himself. He also might be the most naturally stylish person in the entire group. Montell is setting the fashion standard within DIRTY DEEDS without even appearing to try. The clothes, the presence, the attitude—it is simply part of who he is. In a collective where music, film, and design constantly overlap, that instinct matters. Sound creates the world, but style helps people recognize it. @dkthepuffkidd is another artist helping define the collective’s emerging sound. His music lives somewhere between trap, psychedelia, melody, and the beautifully drugged-out edges of the underground. He has an unusual vocal range and a flow unlike anything the rest of us had heard before. DK is from San Antonio and originally entered our orbit through Danny’s former roommate, affectionately known as Lil Whiskey—not a rapper, just an extremely funny nickname. Mercye heard potential in DK and decided to reach out. Since then, the two have been making music that feels raw, unpredictable, and completely alive. That instinct—to recognize potential and act on it—is central to DIRTY DEEDS. The collective is not based on numbers, status, or whoever already appears successful. It is about hearing something in another person and helping them bring it forward. Mercye is in Austin. I am from Corpus Christi. Caleb is from Weslaco. Danny and DK are in San Antonio. On paper, the distance should make everything more difficult. Instead, it has become part of our identity. We have learned how to create without waiting for perfect circumstances. We work through screens, long drives, late-night calls, voice messages, unfinished exports, and whatever time we can find. Distance has not stopped us from creating. It has not stopped us from becoming close. Most importantly, it has not stopped us from exceeding our own expectations. In 2026, DIRTY DEEDS is preparing to begin releasing music. A preview of that future has already been hiding in plain sight. The song featured in the debut ARCHVE MAGAZINE campaign—the cinematic world of the monkey, the package, and the ICON KEYCHAIN SET—is “Jealousy,” a beautiful unreleased record by Mercye. The song is expected to receive its own release soon, turning what began as the soundtrack to a visual campaign into one of the first public steps toward everything we have been building privately. DIRTY DEEDS is still at the beginning. Much of the music remains unheard, many of the ideas are still being organized, and the full shape of the collective is continuing to reveal itself. But the foundation is already here. It exists in the friendships. In the 15-hour FaceTime calls. In the drives across Texas. In the obscure film conversations, unfinished sessions, spontaneous melodies, strange references, and moments when one person’s idea unlocks something inside everyone else. DIRTY DEEDS is not a group assembled to imitate what is already happening. It is a group of people who found one another, recognized something rare, and decided to find out how far they could take it. The distance has never stopped us.
